in writing. - the impact of the measures discussed must be assessed by analysing the statistics recorded by the commission. in fact, in 2007, 72% of the european population lived in urban areas, which are the key to growth and employment. cities need efficient transport systems to support their economies and the well-being of their citizens. about 85% of the eu's gdp is generated in cities. urban areas today have the task of making transport environmentally sustainable (co2, air pollution, noise), competitive (congestion) and social (demographic change, inclusion, health). meeting this challenge is also essential for the success of the eu's global strategy to combat climate change, achieve the 20-20-20 target and promote cohesion. nine out of ten citizens in the eu believe that the traffic situation in their area needs to be improved. i am convinced that coordinated action at eu level can help strengthen the markets for new clean vehicle technologies and alternative fuels. this can encourage users to eventually opt for cleaner vehicles or modes of transport, to use less congested infrastructure or to travel at different times. i am convinced that these initiatives are aimed at improving our habits in the medium and long term, in line with the economic and industrial development of the union as a whole.
in writing. − in july 2002, the commission adopted a block exemption regulation on motor vehicle distribution agreements, replacing regulation no 1475/95. the main objective of the commission's competition policy is to allow the firms concerned to benefit from a safe zone by adopting block exemption regulations, with the aim of ensuring effective market surveillance. block exemptions therefore contribute to legal certainty and the consistent application of community rules. i would like to point out that the importance of this discussion is, in fact, to outline the basic guidelines of the future legal framework which, after the expiry of the regulation, should govern agreements relating to the distribution of motor vehicles and the related after-sales service. therefore, in defining the appropriate scope of the block exemption for the automotive sector, i urge the commission to take into account the conditions of competition on the relevant markets and the need to make a basic distinction between the markets for the sale of new motor vehicles and the markets for repair and maintenance services and/or the distribution of spare parts. i would stress the importance of supporting such proposals which discourage individual initiatives in favour of competitive competition from retailers and repairers and encourage the development of the sector.
in writing. − the importance of new information and communication technologies (ict) is due to their crucial role in triggering a real revolution in the world of science, not only bringing about the knowledge society but also making a sustainable approach to the use of natural resources accessible. in the light of these considerations, in the specific case of new techniques for energy efficiency, it cannot be ignored that icts are an important resource to ensure that progress goes hand in hand with respect for the planet, ensuring that the cost-effectiveness of savings can benefit both the private and the industrial sphere. the energy saving policy will determine the sustainability of the european social model, which is why i have decided to vote in favour of the report.
in writing. − the european union has for some years now been setting itself important targets in terms of energy saving and reducing carbon emissions. the information and communication technologies (ict) sector is undoubtedly a means of improving the energy efficiency of individual member states. ict can help to control and manage energy consumption, provide new applications and technologies to improve the use of natural resources and cleaner production and industrial processes. the large-scale public consultation launched by the european commission has clarified how icts can contribute to energy efficiency. the european commission has calculated that ict-based systems are capable of reducing energy consumption in buildings - estimated at around 40% of total european energy consumption - by up to 17% and carbon emissions in transport by up to 27%. an urban organisation with the help of ict can substantially reduce its energy impact. the dissemination of good practice and the awareness of local decision-makers about the potential of icts should therefore be promoted.
in writing. − the european union has reaffirmed its commitment to reduce carbon emissions by 20% by 2020. it will be difficult to maintain this commitment without exploiting the full potential of icts. ict can in fact reduce co2 emissions considerably. ict is responsible for 1.75% of carbon emissions in the services sector in europe and produces 0.25% of emissions related to the production of ict-based equipment and consumer electronics. the remaining 98% of emissions come from other sectors of the economy and society. it is therefore desirable to harmonise the methods of measuring and quantifying energy performance in order to have data to develop innovative energy saving strategies and to avoid the phenomenon of 'green misinformation'. in this context, i would like to highlight how icts can play a key role in achieving key objectives, as they are present in almost all sectors of the economy and contribute more than 40% to productivity growth. for these reasons, i reiterate my full support for this strategy which combines adequate economic/industrial development with an eco-sustainable strategy.

textile sector. the new regulation is therefore intended to enable manufacturers, users and consumers to obtain more rapidly innovative products containing new fibres, a subject which is of great interest to european consumers, to the textile and clothing industry and to national administrations. i should like to begin by thanking the committee on the internal market and consumer protection for approving the report on 8 april. i would like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr manders, and the shadow rapporteurs for the thorough and detailed work on this proposal which has resulted in a lively and constructive debate on textile labelling. as this is a proposal for legislative simplification, the commission's original text deviated from the provisions of the directive, which the regulation now under discussion will have to replace. that said, the commission agrees with the vast majority of the amendments proposed in the report adopted by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. we are aware that some amendments, particularly those proposing to extend the scope of the regulation, will be discussed in the council. we will do our utmost to facilitate the interinstitutional debate and to ensure that acceptable compromises are reached. one of these amendments concerns the 'made in' mark of origin, which was not included in the commission's original proposal: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the directive on the protection of consumers. the amendments proposed in this connection refer to the commission's proposal submitted in 2005 on the origin marking of many categories of imported products, including textiles. i will support these amendments, as i have already had the opportunity to stress at the meeting with the committee on the internal market. i shall take the same approach with regard to the amendment proposing the labelling of non-textile parts of animal origin. i would also like to make a few comments on other amendments. as regards amendment no 19, the commission proposal already provided for the exemption of traditional tailors from labelling. however, extending this exemption to all textile products delivered to the consumer as a single product would allow a possibly excessive number of clothing products to be exempted from labelling. the latter sector is one of the main axes of development of european clothing products and these products would thus be exempted from labelling and the exemptions risk becoming excessive. as regards amendment no 63, which aims to remove toys from the list of products excluded from labelling obligations, i would like to remind you that the fundamental issue for toys is safety. the legislation, which is sufficiently detailed, was thoroughly reviewed in 2009 with extensive discussions in the council and the european parliament. as the safety element is already addressed in the ad hoc legislation on toys, our concern is that the addition of such a burden on manufacturers may be disproportionate. as regards the request to examine other possibilities for labelling textile products and clothing, i am committed to launching a broad and open debate with the interested parties on all the other issues that have been raised in the discussions in the european parliament and the council. i thank you for your attention and i shall listen carefully to the comments that will be made during this debate.

in writing. the european union's textile industry, in response to the major economic challenges facing the sector in recent years, has embarked on a long process of restructuring and technological innovation. the report under discussion, by allowing for the harmonization and standardization of aspects of the labelling of textile products, in my view makes it possible both to facilitate the free movement of these products in the internal market and to achieve a high and uniform level of consumer protection in the european union. i therefore share the call on the commission to submit a report to the european parliament and the council within two years of the entry into force of the new regulation on any new labelling requirements with the dual aim of simplifying the labelling of textile products and providing consumers with accurate and comparable information on the properties, origin and size of textile products. in pursuing these objectives, i believe it is necessary to ensure that the extension of the labelling obligation does not lead to an increase in the burden on businesses, in particular small and mediumsized enterprises. there is currently insufficient evidence to demonstrate the effects on human health of allergenic or hazardous substances used in the manufacture/processing of textile products, so i urge the commission to undertake a study to assess the effects.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, increasing the availability of organs, improving their accessibility and safety, raising public awareness, is what the committee on the environment and health of the european parliament has called for in order to shorten waiting lists for transplants. it is therefore necessary to promote biotechnological research and the circulation of organs in the european union, but also to establish a european donor charter, to prevent transplant tourism and to strengthen the fight against illegal organ trafficking by severely punishing those responsible. in order to prevent illegal practices, living donation should be considered only as an extreme ratio, when other avenues such as post-mortem donation are not feasible. for this reason, no form of remuneration should be provided for the living donor, but only compensation covering the inconvenience caused by the intervention, the amount of which will be determined by national legislation. member states should also adopt or maintain strict legal provisions in relation to transplants and non-in-breeding living donors, with the aim of making the system transparent and excluding the possibility of illicit organ sales or coercion of donors. on the other hand, they must guarantee the reimbursement of social costs for living donors and protect them against discrimination, in particular by insurance systems. parliament stressed, however, that living donation should be seen as complementary to donation after death. organ donation needs to remain strictly non-commercial, supporting measures to protect donors and ensuring that organ donation is carried out in an altruistic and voluntary manner.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we are talking today about organ transplantation, which is certainly one of the most positive aspects of progress in health care, but which also raises a whole series of problems with regard to the rights of the donor and the patient, which must be tackled from an ethical, social, legal and economic point of view. it is a question of setting in motion a virtuous path that will tackle the serious imbalance between the need for and the quantity of organs available, without however undermining the principle of free and voluntary donation, thus preventing all forms of commercialisation and illegal trafficking, and guaranteeing the quality and safety of organs intended for transplantation by measures that combine confidentiality with traceability. it goes without saying that in a context of cross-border trade and of significant differences between the transplant systems adopted in the different member states, these objectives can only be achieved by promoting coordination and cooperation. in this connection i believe that it would be very important to set up a european database and to adopt common quality and safety standards. we must be careful not to introduce unnecessary rigidities or create additional bureaucratic burdens that undermine what is already being done properly and effectively. that would not only be contrary to our objectives.
madam president, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today transplantation is often a denied right. there may not be a disease that is so socially and psychologically problematic, but there is a chronic gap between those on the waiting list and those who are receiving transplants. the donation procedure is very delicate from a legal and health point of view and is often weakened by procedures which are generally not very streamlined and fast, and which should instead be strengthened in terms of the response to the needs of the population. the european union must therefore work to ensure effective solidarity and voluntary action, without sacrificing the rigour of the procedures, by promoting the professionalism and the very culture of donation. the adoption of common quality standards is certainly a welcome step forward in a context in which the world health organization can make a further contribution.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, accession to the european court of human rights is a fundamental step for the growth of the union: the two guarantee systems will thus strengthen the protection of the fundamental rights of individuals, both within our 27 countries and outside, if we think of all the member countries of the council of europe. so here is an opportunity not to be missed and that we have been waiting for many years. the doctrine and case law of both the court of justice and the court of strasbourg have long anticipated this moment, or rather laid the foundations for this goal, because it is a goal for me, it is a goal for all of us. i cannot therefore fail to mention the importance of accession for all citizens of the union, who will thus be able to bring an action before the strasbourg court against a european institution or a member state, and will thus be even more protected. i conclude, aware that the autonomy of the two courts remains unchanged, as clearly stated and enshrined in the report - indeed, i congratulate my colleague on this report - and by the will of all of us, apart of course from cooperation between the two institutions, which respect their respective competences.

vice-president of the commission. − madam president, everybody is talking about the stockholm programme. that is a christmas tree with several hundred wishes. i would like everybody to speak about the reality. how were these christmas tree wishes treated before the lisbon treaty? behind closed doors, without much consideration for the citizens and what they want, wish for and expect; in the third pillar, where ministers of the interior were asking neither the european parliament nor the commission, and where the european court of justice had no possibility to intervene. that is where we are starting from: an impossible situation. where de minimis decisions were not even carried out at national level, where citizens did not have the means or the instruments to go to court, to protest and to seek justice. fortunately, we now have the lisbon treaty. there is no third pillar any more. there are commission proposals, codecision, implementation at member state level, control by the european court of justice, but that means also that things cannot be done instantly any more. rules and proposals have to follow the normal way, under which you parliamentarians have asked the commission to conduct its work. first, thorough analysis of what is feasible, what is good, what has added value. second, public consultation, in order to know whether the ideas that we put on the table will be accepted or not by civil society, by industry, by the member states, by the national parliaments, which are now a player in all these questions and which conduct the subsidiarity test. and then, impact assessments, in order to see if what we are doing is the right way. and, only then, we have the definite proposal from the commission. if you want the commission to continue to do as has been done over the last number of years, just tell me, and i will come with a proposal every week. and do you know what will happen with those proposals? they will first be blocked in the national parliaments, and rightly so, because we have to come with serious proposals based on the legal assumptions that what we are doing is strong, is feasible and can be implemented in the member states. i do not want the first proposal we make to be challenged before the court of justice and before the court of human rights. i would like to lead all of us to the way where the citizens will understand that the added value of what we are doing here is of real benefit to them in practical terms. yes, as the commissioner responsible for women’s affairs, i have heard this parliament discussing what we need to do, most of all in order to give legal certainty to women in all our member states, that when they have a problem of violence they will get justice and not the illusion that they hope they will get justice and then they get nowhere and end up with nothing. so here we really have to work together. there are hundreds of measures, which have to be ‘lisbonised’, which have to be taken out of the hole and brought into the light of day, which have to be adapted to the real rules of law – hundreds of measures that do not work. the arrest warrant: ms ludford was just speaking about this. of course it is not carried out in the member states because the construction around the mutual recognition and the mutual trust, which is at the basis of the mutual recognition, has not been built up. colleagues, you cannot do all this without having mutual trust. i am sorry, i cannot by decree insert mutual trust in the heads of the judges all over europe! we have to build this mutual trust in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the purpose of the recast directive on the labelling of energy products is to extend the scope of the information to be included on the label to all products which affect energy consumption and not just household appliances. the directive is part of the energy efficiency action plan and also provides for incentive and public procurement initiatives: it will therefore be at the heart of an integrated and environmentally sustainable product policy. one of the most controversial points was the type of scale to be used to avoid confusion for the consumer: the commission has decided to keep the a to g scale closed, even after the european parliament adopted a resolution to that effect. the energy efficiency class will also be included in all advertising containing information on energy consumption or on the price of products. i therefore agree with mrs podimata's approach and support the report.
in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the energy labelling directive plays a crucial role in achieving the community's target of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020. it is a major added value for both the market and consumers. in fact, the obligation to refer to the energy label in advertisements will put an end to the disinformation of final consumers, providing them with all the information they need to make fully informed choices. at the same time, following parliament's strong insistence, the introduction of an open classification was avoided and the model based on a classification from a to g, which has already proved very useful for consumers, was maintained. in addition, the addition of a review clause also allows for a thorough reassessment, in the light of technological developments and consumer understanding of the label, by 2014 at the latest. this is a further guarantee that the current classification, which is easily understood by consumers, will remain unchanged at least until the review takes place. i therefore wholeheartedly reiterate my full support for the directive.

the committee on budgets - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i speak on behalf of our rapporteur, mr schmidt, who - as president buzek announced at the beginning of this part-session - has resigned as a member of the european parliament to take up posts in his own country, and to whom i extend my greetings and good wishes because he has done a very good job. this report is the fruit of his intentions, which we approved by a very large majority in our committee on culture with only one vote against, and for this, on behalf of mr schmidt, i also thank all the shadow rapporteurs who worked on this report. before leaving for strasbourg, i went to rome on monday to visit a private training centre which is very successful because it is able to place the vast majority of the young people it trains over time. and he said to me, "you know, i'm not going to be a doctor. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. help us also to modernise the relationship between universities and enterprises". and the point of this report is right here: today 20% of young europeans are unemployed and among these, about 30% have a university degree, a high, very high percentage, which raises many questions about how the phenomenon of training young people for entry into the world of work is being dealt with in europe today, in this globalised world. so we wanted to work in this report to improve the link between universities and enterprises by identifying some focal points: first, by giving priority to one of the greatest strengths the european union can have, namely the fact that its citizens can adapt to the constantly changing circumstances of the labour market; the fact that the concept of a job for life no longer exists and that vocational training and retraining are essential today. so the first point was lifelong learning, and the second point that we found to be fundamental is mobility. it is important today, as we emphasize in this report, to stress that mobility between countries and between universities and between businesses is fundamental to achieving greater cooperation between the two worlds and we urge not only to extend and expand individual mobility programmes such as erasmus for young entrepreneurs and erasmus for apprentices, but also to organise postgraduate programmes of european excellence, in cooperation with various universities and with the active participation of businesses. and also, encourage more entrepreneurship in the university. this can be achieved, for example, by introducing a knowledge hub system similar to that currently used in some member states, which allows, in particular, small and medium-sized enterprises to improve their research capacities without affecting the independence, autonomy and public character of the university. the third key point is research, and we consider it essential to promote the transfer of knowledge and the increased mobility of researchers, both in the short and long term, across national borders and between academia and business. and finally, the possibility of extending the good practices which exist in many national states in this respect. i conclude, mr president, by imagining how, through this report and the fine work done by the committee on which we have worked, we are convinced that europe will not win the battle against china or other low-wage emerging countries, but with highly qualified professionals and highly competitive companies and in this process it is of the utmost importance that universities and businesses recognise their interdependence and that authorities at all levels help to develop more efficient ways of cooperation.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, after the first assessment of the lisbon strategy, the european union is already looking ahead to the next ten years. a key priority of europe 2020 is smart growth based on both the knowledge economy and innovation. the key to walking along this road is the integration of secondary and tertiary education with the labour market. the route to be followed brings a renewed focus on the world of work together with learning for personal competence, or the so-called knowledge triangle. europe can therefore ensure its relevance on the international scene if it acts in science and innovation in a more united manner and involving all those who can determine both growth and development. in this sense, university evaluation systems are more than appropriate for establishing and measuring standards of efficiency and quality. it is therefore time to move towards that new dimension of european unity known as the 'fifth freedom' or the free movement of knowledge and talent. the commission's proposal is to make it easier for young researchers to work in the community by establishing links with companies to meet their development needs. to achieve these goals, more investment is needed in programmes such as erasmus. this encourages study outside national territories with certain academic recognition for students.

vice-president of the commission. − madam president, may i thank all the members of this house who have, in a very credible and strong way, supported the area of justice which we have started to build. the european treaty of lisbon gives us the possibility now – by giving us the tools – to move forward step by step, putting in place the rights of the citizens, be it the rights of the convicted, or the rights of the victims. everything is in the pipeline and will come quickly. the question related to more proposals forming part of the road map: yes, after the right of interpretation, which i am sure the house will endorse tomorrow, there will be the right of information, the letter of rights which i will put on the table of this house before summer. that will then be followed by the right to legal advice and the right to communicate with people who are dear to the heart. so you see we are going in a direction which aims to achieve the following: the same high level of rights for all eu citizens wherever they are, whatever their problem. it does not matter whether they are travelling for study, for business or for leisure: they should feel at home, and have the same rights as they have at home, wherever they find themselves in europe. one very important question which has been underlined by several members is the question of language. article 2(1) and article 3(1) state very clearly that the accused person who does not understand or speak the language of the criminal proceedings concerned has to be provided with interpretation and a translation of the documents. now this implicitly means that the language into which the proceedings are translated is the language that this person understands. so in fact it does not concern only european union languages or minority languages. it concerns the language of the person who is in front of a tribunal. i believe that this is only fair because we have to have fair proceedings in order to build the trust of the citizens in our justice system and also, and this is of the utmost importance, in order to ensure the mutual trust of the judges and the prosecutors in neighbouring countries’ systems, which cannot be achieved unless we also have a comparable level of rights. there was one question by mr busuttil and other members about procedures – not about procedural rights, but about internal procedures – due to the coexistence of a member state initiative and of a commission proposal. well i must say that in this case this really did not hamper in any way the swift adoption of a very high-quality and balanced legislative instrument. why did it happen? we are now in a very peculiar period. we are coming out of the third pillar and find ourselves in a normal codecision situation. i suppose that after some months we will have learned how best to utilise the tools which are at our disposal in order to reach the best solutions very swiftly. and when i say reaching the best solutions, i mean in the way we used to prepare such solutions: by having an impact assessment, by also having a call for people to come in and say what they think about our proposals. these are the normal proceedings which we are used to and which will guarantee in the end, via the codecision procedure and after having a public consultation and an impact assessment, that we achieve sound policy. sound policy which then can be implemented at national level without creating more distortions than rights, as unfortunately has happened in the past. but we are here with a new treaty, we are here with a charter of fundamental rights, we are going to become a party to the european convention on human rights. i am very confident that, if we should meet together some years from now, we will say, yes, together we have constructed that area of justice and fundamental rights which our continent must become.
in writing. the proposal for a draft framework decision sets out fundamental obligations on the basis of the european convention on human rights and the case law of the european court of justice. the right to interpretation and translation is essential for those who are facing charges in criminal proceedings and do not know the language of the proceedings. furthermore, under article 6 of the treaty, the union respects fundamental rights as guaranteed by the european convention for the protection of human rights, which enshrines the right to a fair trial. the text under discussion today is satisfactory from a compromise point of view and fully acceptable. in the compromise text, the presidency has safeguarded the essential points raised by the member states as regards the costs of implementing the directive and the transposition period. in view of this, i can only welcome the results achieved in the council and the european parliament: interpretation shall be provided in the suspect's mother tongue or in a language known to the suspect, while translation shall be limited to essential documents and the possibility of oral summaries of key documents shall be considered.
in writing. the european union has set itself the objective of creating a single area of justice, with common rules, a high level of cooperation and at the same time procedural guarantees for the parties. the issue is even more delicate in criminal proceedings, where, given the sensitivity of the matter and often the seriousness of both the fact and the penalty, a high degree of legal certainty and respect for rights is necessary. with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the european union must not only respect the echr, but also rely on it, in accordance with the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, to establish eu-wide rules providing protection for suspects and accused persons. in particular, as regards the right to interpretation and translation, it is essential to ensure that all defendants have the opportunity to have full knowledge of all the documents in the case and to be able to understand and express themselves in their own language with the guarantee of translation and interpretation. it is an essential requirement of the single market that every citizen should have the same rights and enjoy the same rights and guarantees as those enjoyed in his country of origin.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission proposal and the line taken by the rapporteur leave the member states free to choose whether or not to include selfemployed persons in the scope of the directive. this optional scheme is inadmissible and contrary to the union competition rules. by leaving the member states free to choose, road hauliers in some countries, which have already transposed the previous directive 2002/15/ec, would be exposed to direct competition from their community counterparts not subject to the same rules. selfemployed workers could go to a country with different legislation, subject to less controls, and this would cause a serious problem of dumping and therefore a serious distortion of competition. in fact, firms could make greater use of selfemployed workers who can offer their services more flexibly and at reduced costs. it goes without saying that low costs often lead to a reduction in quality and, above all, in safety, which in transport means a serious increase in road traffic risks. in view of this, i consider the proposal unacceptable and contrary to one of its legal bases, article 153 of the treaty, because it does not improve the working environment and does not protect the safety and health of workers.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as we know, the european parliament is called upon to give its final word on food information to consumers. it must be said at once that this was a legally laborious, long and controversial process which could not be shortened. the aim is to harmonize community food law by means of legislation which makes information transparent for consumers and avoids making them make confusing or potentially harmful choices. the report by mr sommer, whose efforts to summarize the many needs must be acknowledged, is therefore intended to remedy the controversies and the different information systems in force in the countries of the union. it is no accident that national regulations still differ in the names of the nature of the foodstuffs put on sale, creating a system which differs from country to country and also encouraging unfair competition to the detriment of potential consumers. the aim was to give a new face to existing legislation, involving the food industry on the one hand and consumers on the other, on the basis of the european commission's proposal. the report also calls on the european food industry to clarify mandatory labelling and the indication and presentation of nutritional values. in a globalised market, the european union could not refrain from adapting and innovating its food legislation to better protect food trade and to safeguard it against increasingly invasive and unbridled international competition. it is not new that we hear more and more about the dangers of food products which are surreptitiously labelled and labelled in ways that often do not meet the food requirements and which are nevertheless marketed as beneficial to human health.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i thank the rapporteur. efficient food labelling is indeed very important. the consumer must know what he is eating and he must know it in the short time available to him in the supermarket to make a purchase. but the information must be in a way that is not just understood by a trained food engineer. the aim of this information is to reach a completely different group of people, not those who already have a great deal of knowledge about the health of food. i think one area is particularly important, namely the area of handicrafts and, in particular, the products processed and marketed directly by the farmer. these products are often not standardized in content - think of marmalades or juices, for example - and it is simply not possible to give an exact sugar content or, for example, an exact fuel content. we've been working a lot in the last few years to create shortcuts from farmer to consumer, and things like farm life, farmers' markets and so on are very important now for the image of farmers and agriculture as a whole. in the context of rural development, we have also spent european money to promote such things. in addition, there is a direct link between farmers and buyers in these sales, and this is often more important than the information on the labels. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support the amendments which seek to find a sensible solution for this group of sales.

in writing. - the langen report proposes a series of measures which should make the derivatives market more transparent. given the origins of the 2008 financial crisis and the fragility that markets still suffer from such complex products, it is certainly desirable to try to introduce more stability and transparency. i therefore vote in favour of the langen report. however, we should insist on another point, which is a point of principle, a basic point in the reasoning of finance, of economic and market crises. the 2008 crisis, which cascadingly caused the negative effects that still weigh on our societies today, before derivatives and intricate financial engineering, is caused by the fact that for too long, we mistakenly thought we could do without the real economy. so, while we welcome measures to promote transparency in financial markets and in the products offered by banks and stock markets, let us all remember that there is an urgent need for a general rethinking of the economic system on which world markets are based. the european union must be able to take action to ensure that the european union is able to take action in the field of education and training.

in writing. − the evolution of information and communication technology (ict) has brought about a real revolution in the field of knowledge over the last two decades, mainly thanks to the widespread use of the internet and the world wide web. after networking knowledge and eliminating any distance in the exchange of information, the new frontier of this technology is the possibility of combining a new radio frequency identification system and products, so that they can instantly release information to consumers. i am in favour of deepening the ethical and social implications of this new information resource, which could in future represent a new employment sector, also by implementing pilot projects, and i therefore support the report by mrs maria badia i cutchet.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. the development of the application of the internet of things represents a great opportunity for growth and competitiveness on the one hand, and on the other hand it brings about a great social change, significantly affecting the behaviour of citizens. i therefore welcome the commission's intention to publish a communication on privacy and trust in the information society in 2010, as i believe it is essential to monitor the protection of personal data on an ongoing basis. the debate on the technical and legal aspects of the right to silence of the chip is equally important. furthermore, for the profound changes that the internet of things will bring, it is essential to allow for a uniform development of technologies at territorial level, to avoid creating even larger gaps than those that exist, by adequately involving public authorities in this process and paying attention to the most peripheral areas. finally, i think it is important to increase european funding for the internet of things in the context of research projects under the seventh framework programme and pilot projects under the competitiveness and innovation framework programme, also focusing on infrastructure development, broadband deployment and further reducing data roaming costs.
in writing. - i can only vote in favour of the report by mr sosa wagner on the need to ensure ethical and secure governance of the internet. the tool which has eliminated the distances and times of communication, together with its enormous potential for benefit, is at the same time a daily source of risks, both for the protection of personal data and for minors. it is essential to ensure the free flow of information and communication, but with the certainty that the most vulnerable and sensitive data continue to receive adequate protection. only in this way can the internet continue to be a force for positive social change that respects the dignity of the individual.
in writing. the internet has now become an essential tool in the development of the internal market, which is the pillar of growth and development in the european union. moreover, the percentage of the european population with access to the information world is now over 60%. it therefore seems necessary for the union to play a leading role in the debate on internet governance, thus ensuring that a service that has become central to social and commercial interaction takes due account of the union's own values such as respect for consumers and minors. i therefore support the content and proposals of mr sosa wagner's report.

in writing. − innovations, whether in products or processes, whether radical or incremental, are today the driving force behind the competitiveness of modern business and economic systems that are committed to efficiency and sustainability. research, which is the basis of all innovative action and discovery, must therefore be supported, especially when it brings small and mediumsized enterprises and the world of new technologies closer together. i therefore support mr winkler's own-initiative report, which calls for a third party to complete the knowledge triangle, namely consumers. in a fluid context such as that represented by modern reality, we need reference points. it is therefore important that the growth and competitiveness of the economic and social system also remain "on a human scale".
in writing. - mr president, i voted in favour of this report. i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr winkler, on his excellent work. innovation and research, as well as education and training, are key building blocks for europe to compete positively in a more technologically competitive world. however, only 1% of the eu budget has been allocated to this sector so far, which is insufficient for the difficult challenges facing europe. it is time for the european union to invest more in research and innovation. i am convinced that the economic crisis can be overcome by more funds. i also believe that private investment in technological innovation should be encouraged and stimulated, because only by implementing research can we have a competitive market able to resist the growing trend towards relocation. finally, i agree with the need to provide for 'ad hoc instruments for the innovation capacity of enterprises' and a reduction in the bureaucratic burden for small and mediumsized enterprises, which promote decisive technological innovation.
in writing. − intelligent growth based on the knowledge and innovation economy requires concrete measures by supranational and national institutions. the strengthening of policies to support entrepreneurs in research must be accompanied by policies to encourage investment in new experimentation, including to prepare the skilled labour force to compete in the european labour market. while we ask countries to invest more in research, we must offer them a european regulatory framework, both general and specific, with common and coordinated development guidelines and adequate instruments for monitoring the effectiveness of funding. i agree with the proposal to regulate at european level the measures for apprenticeship, training and vocational training which some countries have already introduced in their school systems, as well as the measures for 'rights and duties' in the field of education. in order to achieve a 3% of gdp target for research funding, however, greater guarantees are needed, such as the academic productivity of teachers, avoiding the fragmentation of resources which has led in recent years to an improper and incongruous use of the already limited funds, with unsatisfactory results. finally, i share the need to have a single court system for patents, in order to standardize titles at the supranational level.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, every year almost 8 million children die before they are five years old. three and a half million die soon after birth from complications of pregnancy. as many as 4 million die in just five countries: india, nigeria, the democratic republic of congo, pakistan and china. many of these deaths could easily be prevented by simple gestures such as breast-feeding, the use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, and vaccines to combat mainly pneumonia and malaria. many mothers are unaware of the importance of vaccines or, even when they are aware, are so poor that they cannot afford transportation to the doctor's office or the hospital. to give these children a future, it does not require huge investments, just bringing in these countries drugs that are very cheap and that for us are part of the normal prophylaxis, building drinking water wells, providing simple mosquito nets and getting what is needed where it is needed. so, above all, we need the political determination to act to save so many lives, to stop this silent slaughter of innocent children whose only fault is that they were born in a poor country.

member of the commission. − madam president, let me thank you first of all for a very substantive and responsible debate and for your draft resolutions on europe 2020 and economic governance. i also want to thank you for your support for the work the commission has been doing, especially in the fields of financial market reform and the reinforcement of economic governance. i would also like to thank diego lópez garrido and his team and the spanish presidency for their excellent cooperation and extraordinary performance during these very difficult times in europe with the most severe financial crisis and economic recession for ages. it has been a great pleasure to work with you and i highly appreciate that. of course i want to wish the best of success for spain today. i could wish some success for switzerland as well but only once they have joined the european union! tomorrow’s european council will take place in a rather dualistic economic situation. on the one hand, economic recovery is in progress and is increasingly gaining momentum, even though it is still gradual and fragile. on the other hand, the turmoil in the sovereign debt markets has cast a serious shadow over financial stability in europe, which could, at worst, derail the still nascent recovery of the real economy. the european union has taken coordinated and determined action to prevent a financial meltdown, but we are certainly not yet out of troubled waters. we must stabilise and reform our economies to pursue sustainable growth and create the jobs europe badly needs. that is what our citizens expect from their leaders. the european council must show the way and take bold decisions to this effect tomorrow. in that context, it is particularly essential to reinforce economic governance in europe. we need to upgrade preventive budgetary surveillance to avoid future crises, we need to address macroeconomic imbalances to go to the root of the problems and we need to construct a permanent mechanism for crisis management. all in all, it is high time to feel at ease with life in the emu and to create a genuine economic union to accompany the monetary union that already exists. the european council made a very important decision when it asked president herman van rompuy, in conjunction with the commission, to set up the task force to suggest ways and means to enhance economic governance. tomorrow president van rompuy will give a progress report on the work of the task force and the first set of orientations. the commission’s communication of 12 may has provided a solid foundation for the work of the task force. there is broad support for our initiatives and we shall follow them up shortly with concrete reform proposals. we must now seize the moment to complete the construction of the economic and monetary union. i count on your support in this regard. i count on your support for our proposals and for the community method, which we have to maintain and further reinforce in this context. let us keep up the momentum, get results and have the new system functional already by the beginning of next year. concerning the toronto summit, the overarching theme should be to strive for unity, redress the problems we are facing, reinforce confidence in the global economy and safeguard economic recovery. i took part in the preparatory meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in busan, korea, two weeks ago and i shall also accompany president barroso to the toronto summit. there will be three priority issues in toronto. quite briefly on this, the first is fiscal consolidation. there was an important change of tone in busan in the meeting of the finance ministers and governors. they agreed that the advanced countries, especially the most vulnerable ones, need to accelerate fiscal consolidation. from the eu side we made it clear that, given the debt levels around the industrial world – in the us and japan they are higher than in europe, for the moment – the fiscal problem is a global problem and not one limited to the eu only, and this problem needs to be addressed as such. europe’s strategy of coordinated and differentiated fiscal exit was recognised, and indeed endorsed, by our g20 partners and the g20 ministers therefore agreed on the need for differentiation very much in line with the european union approach. secondly, the g20 must also aim at rebalancing global demand. this will put the world economy on a more sustainable and higher growth path as we come out of the crisis and for that it is essential that we tackle global imbalances, especially between the us and china. the third major issue is of course financial market reform. there has to be a real step forward at the toronto summit, given its importance for global stability and also for the credibility of the g20. therefore, the g20 in toronto should carry through the rules agreed on improving bank capital, taking action on non-cooperative jurisdictions, and reforming the derivatives markets. in particular, we need a strong message from toronto on bank levies and the g20 needs to show that it is coordinating and delivering on this. no consensus was reached in busan, korea, on the idea of such a levy on financial institutions to foster financial stability and strengthen the resolution framework but, on the other hand, there was agreement on developing a common set of principles on burden sharing. it is indeed essential that the public sector should not bear the cost of the financial sector’s failures, and the principles should also reflect the possible costs of resolution and incentivise appropriate behaviour. the finance ministers also agreed that further progress on the financial repair of the banking and financial sector is critical for global recovery. these discussions will continue in toronto, and i can say from the point of view of the european commission that we are in favour of broad transparency over the bank stress tests, which are essential to restoring and reinforcing confidence in the european economy. in conclusion, for both the european council and the g20 it is now high time for delivery on a smart strategy over fiscal exit, growth enhancing, balancing and reforms, financial market reforms and reinforcing economic governance. it is essential that the european council and the g20 now rise to the occasion and concretely deliver at this critical moment for the european economy as well as for the global economy.

on behalf of the efd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, russia will be a strategic partner of great importance to the european union and it is therefore essential to reach a comprehensive partnership and cooperation agreement. this agreement is a priority for our extra-european policy because it would create the right basis for full cooperation with moscow. i am thinking of bilateral trade, visa liberalization, the control of illegal immigration, the fight against terrorism and organised crime and climate change, as well as particularly urgent issues such as the iranian nuclear issue, the pacification of the caucasus and the middle east peace process. the european union should abandon some of its prejudices and act more concretely and coherently in the energy field. if we are to solve the problem of security of energy supply, we must recognize the added value of the south stream project, which provides a safe and abundant energy route for the economic recovery of the coming years. in its relations with an important partner like russia, europe should operate on two different planes: the european parliament has been a party to the treaty of rome since the beginning of the century, and it is not the council that is responsible for the decisions it takes.

let us proceed with the explanations of vote.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i voted in favour of this report because i believe that european consumers have a right to know what is in the food they eat. the commission's proposal for the recasting of community rules on food labelling is clearly intended to improve legislation on the subject. the aim is certainly to reduce red tape and create greater legal certainty for those involved in the food chain, to increase the competitiveness of the european food industry and to ensure that consumers have in-depth information on food products. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are applied in the community. in our view, the commission has oversimplified matters. i support the rapporteur's proposal on nutritional profiles, which are defined in detail but without any rigidity of scientific evaluation. in general, we cannot understand why the commission has drawn up this proposal for a regulation without recourse to the scientific expertise of experts. it is also incomprehensible that the proposal should be tabled at a time when individual scientific studies are available in certain areas and a wide-ranging investigation covering all the member states has just been launched.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on the sommer report i voted against the amendments introducing the so-called 'traffic light system'. i think that the indication of fats, salts, sugars, saturated fats and energy intake, through a simple system of matching a value, would not give the consumer correct information. there is a real risk that prepared foods, such as frozen pizza, would be penalized by having a red label because they contain cheese. paradoxically, traffic lights favour less healthy products over quality products. finally, i disagree with the calorie labelling of alcoholic beverages, including wine. clarification was given as to the place of origin and provenance of the products.
in writing. − when national and community synergies have the potential to unlock the synergy between research, competitiveness and innovation, i believe it is the responsibility of those who administer and decide to support the project. in the case of the report by mrs lena ek, measures are proposed to coordinate scientific research activities for the understanding of the interactions of the baltic sea ecosystem which are now based on national programmes. i shall therefore be voting in favour of this report.
in writing. - mr president, i share the commission's proposal, which many member states have called for, to establish enhanced cooperation in the area of the law applicable to divorce and legal separation in marriages. it is an important milestone in creating a clear regulatory framework and in providing support to spouses of different nationalities. the goal is to reduce the discomfort for the children and to protect the weaker spouse. this will encourage mediation solutions to avoid long and painful legal proceedings. as the european parliament's ombudsman for children in disputes between parents of different nationalities, i am convinced that this proposal for a regulation will encourage amicable solutions in the interests of children, by defining the duties of parents towards them and the conditions best suited to safeguarding the welfare of the children involved. the proposal also encourages the protection of the weaker spouse by preventing the so-called 'court-race' in which the other spouse seeks to ensure that the divorce proceedings are governed by a law in his or her favour. but above all, the proposal ensures, through a european judicial network in civil matters, access to up-to-date information on the essential aspects of national and union law and divorce and separation procedures to make both spouses aware of the consequences of their choices.
in writing. - although the procedure seems to have been defined, the merits and timing of estonia's accession to the single european currency do not allow me to vote in favour of the report to the house. the european economy is in a period of crisis and turbulence which should prompt us to consider whether new entrants to the euro area are appropriate, at least in the short term. my convictions, which are also based on social and cultural considerations in relation to estonia, are reinforced by some macroeconomic data. estonia was among the first countries to declare recession. in 2009 its gdp fell by over 14% while industrial production collapsed to - 33,7%, the largest contraction in the european union. this negative trend has not stopped. finally, it is paradoxical that, in the face of these figures, the report under vote asks the commission to simulate the effect of the euro area rescue package on the estonian budget only after the country has joined it and thus become a member of the group guaranteeing the rescue fund. this information should be available as soon as possible for the council to take an informed decision and to anticipate future scenarios.
in writing. - i consider the european parliament's motion for a resolution containing the observations which form an integral part of its decision on discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the european union for the financial year 2008, section ii - council, to be of fundamental importance. the proposal refers to the council's lack of involvement in the discharge procedure, which refuses to take part in parliamentary discussions on the matter, thus showing a certain disregard for parliament's role in the discharge procedure, but above all for the right of citizens and taxpayers to demand accountability from all those responsible for the commitment of union funds. the latter is particularly important to me, given that the member states in the council manage about 80% of the actual expenditure of the union budget. i fully support the request that is expressly made to the council, as i consider it necessary that the council should provide detailed information on the nature of the expenditure resulting from the exercise of specific tasks and that its expenditure should be subject to the same checks as those made for the rest of the union institutions, in the framework of the discharge procedure provided for in article 319 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union.
in writing. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the transport of dangerous goods by road. this is a text which, by leaving the member states free to decide, would in fact exclude selfemployed persons from the scope of the directive itself. the exclusion of selfemployed would have introduced substantial discrimination in favour of this category of road hauliers, producing unfair competition between undertakings, increasingly oriented towards using more flexible and cheaper selfemployed workers, and entailing serious risks to road safety. furthermore, it should be noted that italy, in line with directive 2002/15/ec which provided for the inclusion of self-employed hauliers as from 23 march 2009, has transposed this clause in a timely manner by means of legislative decree no 234 of 2007, subjecting self-employed hauliers and employees to the same rules. for these reasons, together with my colleagues from the pdl delegation, i strongly supported the rejection of the european commission's proposal.
in writing. - we cannot accept that selfemployed workers should be excluded from the scope of the directive on the working time of road hauliers. this decision would pose serious risks to road safety, which would be compromised not only by excessive driving times but also by excessive accumulation of non-driving activities. moreover, such a decision would lead to unfair competition between transport undertakings. the use of selfemployed workers would be encouraged, who, thanks to greater flexibility, could offer services at lower costs. the exclusion of selfemployed workers could also have the counterproductive effect of pulverizing transport enterprises, with consequent market distortions. in order to avoid the directive, structured enterprises could be split up into a myriad of small enterprises. the compromise approach of leaving the member states to decide for themselves is also to be rejected, because this too would create the conditions for unequal treatment between persons belonging to different states but exercising the same occupation. i therefore voted in favour of this. moreover, discrimination between road hauliers is totally contrary to the objective of establishing a common transport policy.
in writing. - my position on the report to the house is based, among other things, on the following considerations. the report's subject, directive 2002/15/ec, does not regulate road safety but sets out rules on the organisation of activities additional to driving. the subjecting of self-employed road hauliers to these rules, which is being discussed today, is first and foremost a serious breach of freedom and autonomy of undertaking. secondly, there are obvious practical reasons for not being able to carry out checks on the actual compliance of autonomous road hauliers with the provisions of the directive, which ultimately makes their subordination to the provisions of directive 2002/15/ec unnecessary.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report, although i still have some doubts about some aspects. i believe it is essential to simplify food labelling, allowing consumers to better understand the ingredients, the use and the traceability of the products. i do not agree, however, with the way in which we should achieve this. consciousness in the purchase of products is not increased by the indication of nutritional profiles, guidelines and traffic light systems. these are methods which have no scientific basis and therefore cannot be considered reliable. i am therefore satisfied with the rejection of the traffic light system, but not as satisfied with the adoption of the nutritional profiles and guidelines. finally, i support the adoption of the amendment calling for the specification of the origin of certain foodstuffs. i am a strong supporter of the indication of the origin of products, because i believe it is essential to inform the consumer of the origin of what he is buying. i hope that at the second reading we can agree on a more common text, which better balances the interests involved, health on the one hand and the food industries on the other.
in writing. − the proposal for a regulation has launched a legislative process on a subject which is of fundamental importance to citizens and businesses in the european union, such as transparency and the dissemination of information on food products. while an internal market in which all citizens and all businesses can make the best possible choices is important, it is also important to take account of the extraordinary heritage of food and wine culture that many parts of europe have in their tradition, in favour of health and economic, social and environmental sustainability. the amendments to the proposal, both in detail and in the relevant parts, have shown that the european parliament, in carrying out this fundamental function of exercising its powers, becomes the place where the interests of multinationals are dealt with, to the detriment of those of consumers. in the face of this asymmetry of power, which the pursuit of the public interest by the institution should be accompanied by, it is not surprising that citizens are increasingly distracted from the process of european integration. these observations are not motivated by national interests but by the need to preserve the specific nature of food production and the strong relationship between producers and consumers in the area.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the issue of food information for consumers, which is the subject of mr sommer's report, deserves particular attention. it is by providing clear and comprehensive information on the origin and content of products that the consumer is protected from the risk of making uninformed consumer choices, with possible adverse effects on health. the question is also linked to the policy of protecting quality products and to a general line of action in defence of the consumer, which has been discussed on several occasions both in the plenary and in the committee on agriculture. i congratulate the honourable member on the work she has done on the commission document and i generally agree with the amendments she has proposed, particularly the opposition to the introduction of the so-called 'traffic light' labelling system, which is simplistic and misleading. under this system, some natural and quality products would be penalized compared to others artificially modified in order to obtain a green badge. i consider it an important achievement to have extended the obligation to indicate the origin also to the primary ingredients in processed products, whereas i would have liked a negative vote on the derogations to the methods of classifying products, because they risk rendering the whole legislation ineffective.
in writing. - my position on the report to the house is based, among other things, on the proposal to introduce a multi-colour labelling system. the quality of food depends on many complex factors which cannot be represented appropriately by a different colour on the label. according to authoritative studies on the subject, there are no numerical thresholds for an accurate division of foodstuffs between the different colours proposed. therefore, the adoption of a multi-colour labelling system would unduly influence the assessments of consumers who should instead be able to make their own choices on the basis of transparent information.
in writing. - mr president, i listened with interest to the reports by commission president barroso and president van rompuy. while i welcome the improvements in european economic governance towards a common approach, i sincerely believe that the outcome of the summit is merely declarations of intent. in fact, at this particular moment in history, it is necessary to create a more solid common basis for dealing with the budget deficits of individual states and restoring the confidence of the financial markets and our citizens. i certainly share the objective of the eu 2020 strategy, which is to strengthen the competitiveness of the 27 member states. it will be crucial, if we are to win this challenge of future economic leadership, to have clear rules that are workable for everyone. we must avoid making the same mistakes as those made with the lisbon strategy, with consequences for citizens, jobs and economic growth.

author of the book. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, article 5 of the universal declaration of human rights states: "no individual shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment". this prohibition applies in all circumstances and is a peremptory norm of international law and as such applies to all states. not only the universal declaration of human rights but also the united nations convention and the european convention seek to protect human rights against torture. the european union and its member states take these obligations very seriously. we also consider that the fight against torture is a top priority for the european union, given that next week we will be celebrating the international day against torture. it is precisely in order to comply with these very important legal and moral obligations that trade in material intended for the purpose of torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment needs to be closely monitored. the adoption of the regulation was a major step forward at the time of its adoption, as was also confirmed by the un special rapporteur on the fight against torture. moreover, this regulation is a model in terms of international legislation on the subject. unfortunately, the application of this regulation has not been as exemplary as the adoption of the regulation itself: only seven member states submitted one or more of the annual public reports provided for in article 13 of the regulation containing detailed information on the authorisations granted for the import and export of goods which could be used for torture. these reports are an essential element in assessing full compliance with the regulation. an analysis of the authorisations granted raises a number of questions about the end-use and destination of the goods. the authorities responsible for authorising exports must therefore carry out a more thorough policy assessment before proceeding. the member states which have also communicated information on the penalties applicable for infringement of the provisions of the council regulation, as provided for in article 17 thereof, are not many. almost five years after the adoption of the regulation, the list of goods identified in the annexes to the regulation needs to be updated. man can be very cruel, and at times it seems that the human imagination for inflicting suffering on others is limitless. so it is vital to keep up with the technological developments in this sad area. the time has therefore come to raise the issue in the european parliament and to ask the european union and its member states to demonstrate that they are living up to their commitments. as members of the european parliament, it is our democratic duty to ensure that the institutions are accountable. that is why we want detailed information on what has been done so far to ensure full compliance with the regulation, but also on the measures that will improve the situation in the future. we welcome, as a first step, the decision of the committee overseeing the application of the regulation at the end of this month. let us never forget that council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, bosnia-herzegovina is the country in the western balkans which has made the least progress in meeting the criteria suggested by the european commission, despite being the region where the international community and the european union have been most present, with ad hoc institutions and financial aid. bosnia and herzegovina is still facing major difficulties. the european union cannot envisage the future accession of a country where the high representative is still present and actively involved in the political decision-making process. progress will therefore depend to a large extent on a gradual process of the representative office. it is not clear how the various political partners can work together. the country is divided between the republic of serbia and the federation, and is also divided into three main ethnic groups, each representing a minority in its own part of the territory. as a result, the population has declined over the past decade from 4.5 million to 3.4 million. it seems that the people themselves are no longer convinced that there is a future for their country. the prospect of accession to the european union was offered to bosnia and herzegovina by considering it as a single country and not as separate territorial parts. in bosnia-herzegovina, therefore, a decision must be taken whether to join a single country before any further consideration of membership can be made.
member of the commission. − mr president, thank you for grounding me from air to rail now. it is my privilege to stand before parliament to speak on this matter. i would like to thank parliament very much for its support for the efforts of the european commission to control the proper implementation of the first railway package by member states, which is their responsibility. the commission, for its part, has complied with its obligations as guardian of the treaty by sending reasoned opinions to 22 member states for incorrect implementation of the first package. i can assure you that the commission will not hesitate to take member states which are still not complying with european legislation to the court of justice. while the specific legal details of the infringement procedures are a matter between the commission and the member states, our services have already submitted to the committee on transport and tourism, earlier this year, a complete list of all infringements. we also share the regret expressed by the committee that the level of investment in rail infrastructure remains insufficient in many member states. however, the commission cannot agree with the statement that it has not sufficiently focused monitoring on the financial foundations of the railway system. the directives of the first railway package only prescribe that member states have to ensure a balanced budget for the infrastructure managers over a reasonable period of time. where the commission has found evidence that member states have not respected this provision, infringement procedures have been opened. some interest groups want to go further and think that the commission could oblige member states to increase investment in the railway sector in general. we might like to see this, but there is no legal base to support it. that being said, the commission has, on several occasions, made a political appeal to member states because we recognise the importance of investment in rail infrastructure to promote a sustainable transport system in europe. not very long ago there was a discussion on that question in this chamber, in the context of the volcanic ash cloud and the implications it had for connectivity within europe and between europe and the rest of the world. i note the wish that the revisions of the first railway package should address the question of lack of resources and powers of regulatory bodies as a priority. i can assure you that the forthcoming commission proposals will do just that. the recast of the first package will also contribute to clarifying principles of infrastructure access charging, in line with the request from parliament. on the independence of essential functions, the commission has already made its position very clear in its communication of may 2006. infrastructure managers must be independent from railway undertakings and railway holdings. a holding should not have operational control over its infrastructure subsidiary. control and independence exclude each other: you cannot have both at the same time. based on the case law of the court of justice, we have established clear criteria for assessing the independence of an infrastructure subsidiary from the holding company. i am therefore confident that the commission will win this argument in the forthcoming court procedures. the resolution also calls for the application of a reciprocity principle. however this is not a principle that we can accept in european legislation in general. each member state has to comply with the european directives as they stand, independently of what other member states do. otherwise implementation would always follow the path of the slowest member state. in conclusion, i acknowledge the critical view the draft resolution takes on the implementation of the first railway package by the member states. i reassure you again that the commission has done – and intends to continue to do – its job as guardian of the treaty. the commission should not be left alone in pushing for rail market opening and, ultimately, for the revitalisation of rail as a sustainable and efficient mode of transport. we count on your support to make european rail policy a full success and a contribution to getting europe out of the present economic crisis.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, it is undeniable that too much time has been lost on the implementation of the first railway package. as is well known, the three directives were adopted in 2001 and were to be transposed into national law by 15 march 2003. in view of the review of the first railway package, i would like to focus, in addition to the investment issue which the commissioner has rightly mentioned, on three concepts which i believe are essential for the proper implementation of the first railway package, three concepts which i think the commission should take into account. first, the various difficulties that have emerged in recent years have revealed issues that need to be clarified regarding the different legal interpretations of the independence of infrastructure managers. i think, madam commissioner, that there is still room for some further clarification on this subject, because it has been one of the obstacles we have encountered in recent years, and i hope that, when the first package is being reviewed, we will finally be able to arrive at a clear interpretation. secondly, i believe that the completion of the liberalisation of the railway market must be seen as the top priority for all member states. as we know, everyone is in favour of liberalization, but few are prepared to try it out in their own countries. for these reasons, the full implementation of the first package is an essential condition for achieving this result. i therefore ask the commission to step up its action in this direction. finally, it is no longer conceivable that undertakings operating under absolute monopoly conditions within their national borders could exploit this competitive advantage to the detriment of competing undertakings in countries which have opened up their internal market. for this reason, while sharing the strategic objective of liberalization, we believe -
