president of the commission. − mr president, i will answer two concrete questions and also make a general remark after the debate that took place this morning. first of all, a question raised by mr schulz: an important one about the irish stress tests. let me say the following. the common methodology of the stress tests was agreed at european level; it was very rigorous, with adverse macroeconomic scenarios. however, the implementation of the tests was carried out under the responsibility of the national supervisory authorities. it was coordinated at european union level by the cebs, but there were no european union competences for that. i want to underline that, until recently, the european union as such did not have this kind of responsibility. this is going to change next january. we will have the new architecture of financial regulation and supervision in place by then, following commission proposals and agreement with the council and in parliament. we will have the three european micro-prudential supervisors for banking, securities and insurance, and the european systemic risk board for macro-financial stability and the risks associated with it. and that will provide much stronger tools and infrastructure to carry out the tests next time in a more unified, rigorous and coherent manner. so i want to underline this point. before the crisis we did not have the instruments that we are creating now. then i come to the second issue concerning the way we are now dealing with some sensitive issues like the permanent crisis mechanism. i want to make it clear that it was not my intention to raise the point but, since there was a concrete question, i have to reply. unanimously – and i repeat unanimously – the heads of state and government decided to ask for a permanent crisis mechanism with the intervention of the private sector. i was one of those who warned the european council about the risks of raising this issue without proper preparation and communication. but the issue was raised and decided and now we have to deal with it in the most responsible way. that is why i believe some of the comments made here today were really not helpful. we are still living in very difficult conditions. i think what we need now is action and not more comments. we are dealing with very sensitive global financial markets. some of the comments sometimes have a self-fulfilling prophecy effect. so it is not helpful to start speculating about countries that may be at risk. what we have to ask those countries is to implement all the measures that are necessary for achieving financial and budgetary stability. that is why i am not going to speculate about plan b. we, together with president van rompuy, are doing our work, discussing the issues with responsibility with our member states. regarding the role of the commission, i want to be extremely clear once again. the commission – and this was acknowledged by most of you – has always been putting forward ambitious proposals. we are for ambitious economic governance for europe. but in the end we have to be realistic. together we cannot go beyond what is established by common agreement with our member states. when there is an agreement – an agreement that anyhow represents progress compared to the previous situation – it is not helpful to speak about ideal solutions that you very well know will not come into effect. so the commission is fulfilling its role, and will fulfil its role, asking for more ambition in terms of common purpose, economic governance, stability of the euro area – and not only of the euro area. i want to make that point very clearly because i think it was not made during this debate today. some of you said the problems are in the euro area. i am sorry to say they are not only in the euro area. the euro has not been the problem. i am absolutely convinced that the situation would be much worse if we did not have the euro. (applause)some of you tend to forget that some countries that are not in the euro area have exactly the same problems, in some cases even worse problems of sovereign debt, and that a country that is not even in the european union and that is now asking to join the european union – iceland – went bankrupt, and they do not have the euro. the reality is that the euro was not the cause of the problem. it is intellectually and politically dishonest to suggest that the problem is with the euro. (applause)what we have to do now is recognise the specificities of the situation in the euro area, to address the problems and ask all the member states to give a commitment to work collectively: those who are in the euro area and those who are not. i think they have all understood that there is a common interest in a common approach to resolve this crisis. that is what the commission will do, in a responsible way, pushing of course for the highest level of ambition, but in the end working in good, loyal cooperation with all the institutions, with this parliament, as we have done, and with the council and european council. that is the responsible method that we have to follow. in a period where markets are extremely nervous, we should keep cool heads and we should keep a strong sense of responsibility, also of course with a strong sense of common european purpose. president of the european council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, earlier it was said that there was a difference between the analysis of the president of the commission and mine, but this is the first time, mr schulz, that i have been accused of singing the song 'all is well, madame la marquise'. it's the first time in my entire career. i can assure you that i do not in any way underestimate the crisis and that we are living in serious times. unless some of my remarks are taken out of context, i am a very cautious man and i think that far too many inflammatory and other statements are being made - not here - in the european context. the time is now for calm and not for a repeat of the depth of the crisis. we know enough. it's time to act. some of you said we should learn from this. there's a french proverb that says, "our deeds follow us". when i took up this office, there was a stability and growth pact, which was made a little more flexible a few years ago and which was not implemented. when i took office, i inherited the lisbon treaty, which provides for certain procedures, among other things, on sanctions, among other things, on the decision to be taken when a country is put under the excessive deficit procedure. the council decides on this, according to the lisbon treaty. when i took office, there was no crisis mechanism. we had to fix all that. we will therefore strengthen the stability and growth pact and introduce a system of macroeconomic surveillance for the first time. i can assure you that if we had had this mechanism a few years ago, the problems in some countries would never have happened. we would have discovered the housing bubbles. we would have discovered the problems of competitiveness of some countries. we're going to introduce him now. it's an innovation, it's a new one. we're learning the lessons of the crisis. as for the lisbon treaty, it is intended to give a permanent crisis mechanism a legal basis, as opposed to certain constitutional courts. that's the only reason. i hope we will not risk reopening a great debate on the institutions, which would lead us nowhere, in my view, in the present context, and would further distance us from the energy we must devote to combating the crisis. there was no crisis mechanism. when we faced the problem of greece, we had to invent a mechanism. there wasn't any. when we took another measure, the 750 billion for the other crisis, we had to interpret the lisbon treaty in a creative way in order to put it into practice. so we are learning all the lessons of the crisis and i say: "our actions follow us". we had a stability pact that was weak and unenforced, we had nothing on macroeconomic surveillance and there was no crisis mechanism. and have our member states taken their responsibilities? many of them have taken up their responsibilities. they engage in reform policies often against the mainstream of public opinion. they often take very courageous action, not only in countries where there is tension but also in other countries. we take responsibility. my dear colleagues, we must not always be mistaken about the enemy. i often get the impression that we are too much directed towards the governments and parliaments of the member states. let's not mistake the enemy. so today, some people are talking not only about ireland but also about portugal, and let me quote the figures here. the government deficit was 9.3 in 2009. it will be 7.3 in 2010. it will be 4.6 in 2011. the average interest rate on portuguese public debt is 3.6%. that's extremely low. the country is not suffering from a housing crisis, a housing bubble. its financial sector is not too high compared to the country. its banks are well capitalized. let's not mistake the enemy. if some say that there is a contagious movement, it is not based on economic grounds, it is not based on rational grounds. i wanted to tell you. let's not mistake the enemy. those who have advocated cooperation between the institutions can be assured that at the level of the presidencies we are doing everything to work together. the report of the task force was approved by its members, including the member of the european commission responsible. and also in other areas, for the permanent crisis mechanism, we work hand in hand. i hope we can return to this spirit when we draw up the 2011 budget. i regret that we were unable to reach an agreement. but speaking of cooperation, let me make a point. you are all members of the european parliament from certain political families. i have to say that there is a very big difference at times between what i hear in the european council, through the prime minister and through the various parties, and what i also hear in this house from the same members of the same political family. that's not a reproach. you don't have to agree with your political party all the way. in my career, i have often witnessed confrontations within my party. in writing. ladies and gentlemen, both greece and ireland have had to resort to eu intervention. there are, however, some distinctions to be made between these two cases. the dublin deficit exploded because the country had to buffer the difficulties of the crisis-ridden banking sector from the backlash of the global financial crisis, exacerbated by the bursting of the housing bubble. this intervention, at a time of structural crisis, meant that public finances could no longer support such a situation. for greece, on the other hand, the reason for intervention is due to a poor management of public expenditure which necessitated an inflow of money from government bonds. in view of the reform of economic governance, the following observation is therefore necessary. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the budget. however, these two cases demonstrate the importance of taking account of all factors relating to the finances and soundness of a state and not just structured public debt. this may be only the final figure, but we must go and see what factors and causes are behind these figures and how we have arrived at such a situation.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of the new legislation on information on medicinal products is a further step towards ensuring that patients have clearer and more effective information on the medicines they take and are prescribed. a harmonised legislative framework at european level is needed which, in addition to maintaining the ban on advertising for prescription medicines, takes account of the 'right of the patient to information'. this is not a small matter, since the sometimes blurred line between "promotion of a product" and "information about a product" can confuse the patient. we must remember that throughout the european union the active role of patients in health care is steadily growing. therefore, better access to non-promotional information can help citizens better understand the treatments they are prescribed and facilitate their recovery, all of which is of course in the interest of their health. in conclusion, i would like to stress the importance of transparently defining the types of information on medicinal products and the channels through which it can be transmitted. the risk of uncontrolled publicity and, if and when necessary, the risk of an excess of uncontrolled and misleading information must be curbed.

on behalf of the efd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although i have announced in advance both in committee and in the house that the copenhagen climate conference and the document presented by this parliament will fail, experience has taught us nothing. if we insist on unilaterally asking europe to reduce its emissions to levels far above those required under kyoto, the next summit in cancún - cop16 - will also be a failure and our parliament will once again make a bad impression. the resolution adopted by the committee not only reiterates that the contribution to developing countries should not be less than eur 30 billion a year by 2020, but also encourages the union to promote the creation of a green climate fund, allocating usd 100 billion a year from 2020 onwards. the document also says how to raise the funds, that is by taxing all possible sources, for example by imposing taxes on financial transactions, on trade and on air tickets, in effect taking this money directly out of the pockets of citizens and businesses. the report then launches into utopian demands. it even calls for a reduction in co2 emissions to the atmosphere by 2020 of 30% instead of 20%, and calls on the commission to come forward with a proposal for the eu to unilaterally set these targets. to ask our people and our businesses to make such sacrifices at a time of economic crisis like the one we are experiencing is yet another euro-craziness. we share the council's view that the european union can only consider a second commitment period under the kyoto protocol if this is done in a comprehensive framework involving all the major economies and with a view to a legally binding global agreement.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, madam president-in-office, the european will to set ambitious targets for the next climate change conference is certainly a commitment to be pursued with tenacity and with the awareness that the results will determine the future of our planet. but that is precisely why, ladies and gentlemen, we must be realistic and more cautious in our expectations. as far as we know, the international negotiations leading up to the cancún conference have not only failed to make appreciable progress towards a comprehensive agreement, but have also confirmed the doubts and resistance to the commitments made in copenhagen. it has been mentioned before, but i would like to mention china here as well. china, for example, is committing to an increase in its emissions of 5 billion tons of co2 by 2020, with consequences that could be offset, and perhaps not even offset, by a 100% reduction in european industrial emissions by the same year, by 2020. this not only makes the proposal for an unconditional 30% reduction, which we strongly oppose, a welcome one, but it also leads many independent observers to assume that global emissions will still increase, even significantly, by that date. in this contradictory situation it would be risky and even demagogic to speculate on numbers and to draw up scenarios which are suggestive but not realistic, where the unknowns are inevitably reflected in the size of the costs. the hope is that the european union will bring a shared, realistic and sustainable proposal to cancún, because an agreement that gives concrete and tangible results is always preferable to expectations that are inevitably destined to fail and to make the efforts of governments on major environmental issues less and less credible in the eyes of international public opinion.

member of the commission. − mr president, i thought i could limit myself to three basic comments after this lively debate, but i find i should firstly respond to a very direct question from mr pargneaux: i think that we can make good progress on the architecture for a green fund. however, for many parties, some of the very specific sources of finance will probably need a bit more looking into – as it is only two weeks since the high-level panel from the un came forward with these various inputs. realistically, we should make substantial progress. we should know what we want to do with this fund and how to set it up. then i am sure, soon thereafter, that we can also deliver on the requirements of the fund. i think we will have to progress gradually, but we are very much in favour of progressing on the green fund. now my three comments. firstly, marita ulvskog said early in this debate that the climate issue has slid down the international agenda this year. that is of course true, but it is also true that if we compare our current position to two ago – or to five or ten years ago – we can see that climate is very much up on the agenda today. were it not for the run-up to the copenhagen accord, can you imagine that the issues on climate change, energy efficiency and how to promote green growth would have survived the economic crisis? i would argue probably not. it is something that this is still very much on our agenda in the eu, and it must also stay there. mr ouzký mentioned that europe is always ‘too optimistic’; well maybe it is not always in vain. it is not the pessimists who achieve big things. by setting targets, europe showed the way in 2008; and in the run-up to copenhagen, a lot of economies followed. two years ago we were more or less alone in setting targets. in the run-up to copenhagen, big economies such as indonesia, mexico, korea, india, south africa and others – the list is much longer – set domestic targets. all other things being equal, this is also very important when seen from a european business perspective. that was something we actually gained. now in a lot of countries, these domestic targets will lead to some kind of paradigm shift. yes, it is too slow in many ways, but actually we have come quite a long way. somebody referred to the emerging economies. this was not an issue for emerging economies before; two years ago the emerging economies would have said that climate change was not for them to deal with. the rich countries would have to deal with it – the developed countries. today, because of author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, there are not many of us here tonight to talk about anti-dumping, which is also a subject of great interest in our countries. i believe that there is no other issue in international trade matters which is more at the heart of businessmen, large and small companies, trade unions and consumers than dumping. the confrontation with dumping is in fact a kind of daily bread for so much of our productive reality. the commission is doing its duty and is certainly doing its duty with regard to anti-dumping measures, but we are asking for action which is guided by the following principles. firstly, the transparency of the action, full transparency of the procedures, the evaluation criteria adopted and the results, and then the communication and a communication strategy, because the anti-dumping actions of the european union commission represent an element of reassurance for our entrepreneurs and our workers. secondly, there is a margin of discretion in anti-dumping proceedings. this is common sense, but sometimes i get the impression that there is too much discretion in the decisions that are taken. thirdly, the european parliament must be more closely associated, involved and informed in the post-lisbon phase. i think there is a certain amount of difficulty on the part of the commission in fully recognising this role of parliament in international trade - member of the commission. − mr president, i am happy that the european parliament shares our view that the defence of eu production against international trade distortions should be considered as a necessary component of an open and fair trade strategy. i share your view that trade defence instrument (tdi) decisions must continue to be founded on technical and factual elements, and i am confident we have one of the most effective and fairest trade defence systems in the world. i am aware that, in anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations, there are many interests at stake and that some stakeholders attempt to influence the decision. nevertheless, i can confirm that the decision-making process is effective, transparent and based on factual evidence and thorough analysis. i acknowledge that third parties have recently tried to influence our decision making by pressuring industries or, indeed, member states and companies operating in these third countries. i strongly condemn such actions. in this context, the entry into force of the lisbon treaty provides an opportunity to address this problem. i would like to assure you that the number of tdi cases remains stable over the medium and long term: so, in response to mr sturdy, no, it is not going up. we have managed to avoid any significant increase which could have happened as a result of the world recession, and have ensured that the anti-dumping instrument would not be used for protectionist purposes. most statistics show that the number of cases in the eu remains lower than in our main trading partners. china remains, by and large, the main source of unfair trade (around 35% of cases launched by the eu are against china). i am determined to take action where necessary, and this includes anti-subsidy action. mr sturdy also put a question with respect to a recent case, the so-called ‘modem case’, where the commission had, in fact, looked at three aspects: the dumping, the subsidisation and also the safeguards. the dumping and the subsidisation were investigated on the basis of complaints by the company concerned and, according to the basic regulations, complainants can withdraw their complaints. eu law stipulates that, where a case is withdrawn, the proceedings can be terminated unless such termination would not be in the community interests. we are currently examining the implications of the withdrawals. it should be pointed out that the commission has accepted such withdrawals in the past and has consequently terminated investigations without taking measures. on the third case, concerning the safeguards, this is, in fact, a complaint initiated by the government concerned in the case – the belgian government – so that is a somewhat different procedure. the company concerned (option nv) has now informed the commission that it has asked the belgian government to withdraw the request for the imposition of safeguard measures, but the belgian government has not yet informed the commission whether it will comply with option’s request, so we are waiting for the belgian government to take a decision on its position. that is precisely what has happened in this case. now, continuing on the broader issues, trade defence instruments are there for good reasons. in the absence of international competition rules and other rules associated with properly functioning markets, trade defence instruments are the only possible means of protecting our industry against unfairly traded goods. we seek to use these rules in the most efficient way for our industries. the existence of time limits ensures quick action for the industry and predictability for exporters. i intend to keep our instruments effective and fair, for the benefit of all the economic operators concerned. the international rules on trade defence are being renegotiated in the world trade organisation (wto). the eu position there is clear: we want to maintain the effectiveness of our instruments while protecting our business against protectionist actions by others. these wto negotiations, as well as changes brought about by the lisbon treaty, are important in relation to any review of our rules that we would wish to undertake. as regards smes, trade defence instruments indeed represent a challenge for smes, in terms of both costs and complexity. there is a need to reduce the administrative burden for smes in trade defence investigations. this is why i have commissioned a study to look at the specific difficulties that smes face when dealing with tdis, and at possible solutions to alleviate these difficulties. regarding the institutional aspects, you will have noted that the comitology proposal submitted by the commission in march provides for parliament to be fully informed as to the committee proceedings. the commission will also provide information on the proposed measures on which the committees are asked to deliver an opinion, the final measures and the final adoption by the commission. at any time, parliament can obtain further information on request. in this context, let me confirm that the commission is effectively ready to make a proposal on the alignment of the trade defence instruments with the new system of control of delegated and implementing acts (this is the so-called ‘trade omnibus’). however, as you are aware, there is significant discussion between the institutions on the overall issue of implementing acts. the commission is carefully following the discussion and gauging, on the basis of contacts with the other institutions, when such a proposal should be adopted by the commission. however, let me be clear that the only issue is that of when the proposal will be made, not whether it will be made. there was also the specific question by mr moreira on the comitology. there, i would like to be very clear. i see no argument whatsoever in the lisbon treaty for having special treatment for comitology when it concerns trade, and we will not agree to that. of course, the decision is in the hands of parliament and the council, although the commission could also have a role to play, as, ultimately, could the european court of justice. introducing a different majority – because that is what it really comes down to – for overruling the commission on questions of trade is not acceptable to us, and it is certainly not acceptable to me. finally, regarding the use of trade defence instruments by third countries, we have indeed observed an increase since the beginning of the economic crisis. i would like to assure you that we follow trade defence actions by third countries closely, and we take action when necessary – including intense monitoring, effective support for eu exporters affected and, indeed, the initiation of dispute-settlement procedures at the wto. in many cases the commission’s actions lead to the termination of the investigation without the imposition of measures. in other cases, these interventions often result in lesser measures being imposed on the eu exporters concerned. there was also a question about possible forms of retaliation towards third countries in respect of pressures exerted on european companies. we have received petitions on this matter from european companies but we do not disclose their names, in order to protect them. for example, in a recent case involving china, china attacked the dispute settlement in the wto and the panel supported us, but we have not made public the names of the companies concerned, and i think this was also to protect the companies. two final questions were on whether we are going to review the trade defence instruments. we are not, because i truly believe it is not necessary. there is an enormous amount of work to be done on trade in the coming years, and i must say that i do not want to reopen certain discussions through such a review process. i would consider doing so only once the doha round is over. there was also a specific question by the green member. mr schlyter, your question is an interesting one, i must say, because, as you most probably know, these anti-dumping cases are introduced by companies. they are taken on the basis of a complaint by a company. so if a company were to raise the issue that you put forward concerning carbon leakage, then the commission would, of course, investigate and see whether the case ought to result in measures being imposed. but the issue is certainly not beyond the scope of the arguments that we consider. we consider the arguments that are put forward by the companies concerned, so if a company were to put this before us then we would certainly look into the matter.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, anti-dumping, which is one of the most effective instruments for defending the fairness of trade in the union in order to compete fairly on the market, needs clear rules that can be applied within the new comitology. the treaty of lisbon clearly states that the commission is responsible for implementing acts. the council, together with parliament, has the power to scrutinise the commission's work. the compromise under discussion today actually deprives parliament of the role that lisbon has assigned to it and could thus create a new democratic deficit within the institutions. in particular, we do not understand and reject the proposal to reserve a differentiated treatment for anti-dumping measures, a treatment which introduces elements of discretion, politicization and legal uncertainty into proceedings whose purpose should instead be to protect the legitimate interests of companies harmed by unfair competition practices. at a time of severe economic crisis such as the one we are experiencing, it seems to us unreasonable and self-destructive to make the conclusion of anti-dumping proceedings in fact complicated and perhaps impracticable. this is what the present proposal would be if it were not amended. we appeal to the sense of responsibility of the member states, as well as of the commission, member states whose common interest must be to ensure greater development. development is possible only if there are rules which prevent market distortion, respect institutional roles and make procedures fast.
the number of anti-dumping procedures applied by the european commission has increased in recent years. this is the signal of the increase in unfair practices by other countries towards european companies. despite the economic and financial crisis, 332 protectionist measures have been adopted by international partners in the last two years. we believe in free but fair international trade, based on the sharing of equal rules for all. it is important to safeguard the effectiveness of european trade defence instruments which act to correct situations of illegality. i am deeply concerned about the effect that the current attempts to reform comitology will have on the effectiveness of these instruments. leaving room for political and diplomatic negotiations to decide on the application of anti-dumping measures risks distorting a process which must instead remain based on concrete and objective data.

in writing. − we support the human rights and social and environmental standards in international trade agreements, because too often third countries that do not respect workers' rights and do not agree to be active in the fight against climate change are unfairly competing with eu companies. our companies must comply with very strict standards of worker protection and high levels of both wage and tax contributions, they must comply with laws that impose strict controls on emissions into the environment and they must comply with conditions set by local regulatory plans. it is clear that competing companies in other third countries, such as china and india, are not subject to the same controls and rules and have a final product that is clearly competitive with the european one. speaking in the committee on the environment and the interparliamentary meeting on energy, i called for the eu to be involved in the wto, so that europe could apply a carbon tax to countries that are not signatories to climate change agreements. the same should apply to countries which produce by methods too different from those in europe, for example by using child labour, or which do not recognise the rights of workers.
in writing. − the report on the activities of the european ombudsman's office in 2009 is of great interest, as it allows us to assess whether and to what extent the relationship between the community institutions and citizens is transparent, agile and effective. there are many issues on which parliament and the commission express their views without receiving any other feedback from citizens than the reports made to the ombudsman. however, while i approve of the report, i believe that the figure of the european ombudsman, as well as his functions, should be more widely publicized, especially in the member states where he is not immediately recognizable. in fact, it should never be forgotten that a small number of complaints can mean both a low perception of wrongdoing and a low confidence in a possible judicial solution to problems. more publicity would make it possible to extend the case-study at the methodological level, so that it would be possible to state with greater confidence which of the two situations outlined is the case.
in writing. − the european ombudsman's objective is to ensure that citizens' rights, as enshrined in community law, are respected at all levels of the union and that the work of community institutions and bodies is conducted in accordance with the highest administrative standards. recently, his collaboration with the european network of ombudsmen has enabled him to continue implementing a programme to improve the quality of information provided to citizens and potential complainants about their rights. it must continue to work to ensure that citizens' needs are at the heart of all the work of the eu institutions and bodies and must therefore pursue every opportunity to reach an amicable settlement of disputes by launching new investigations on its own initiative to identify problems and promote good practice. i supported this report because it is intended to encourage the ombudsman to continue to work with the institutions to promote good administration and a culture of service and to step up communication efforts so that citizens who need to use his services are properly informed about this, thereby strengthening their trust in the eu and its institutions and improving our own credibility.
in writing. - ladies and gentlemen, since the protection and respect of human rights is a key issue for the european union, it is clear that the role of the european ombudsman cannot be overlooked in this area. that is why i voted in favour of mrs nedelcheva's report, because the role of the european ombudsman as a promoter of respect for citizens' rights cannot be ignored. this important figure at european level works to ensure that citizens' needs are at the heart of all the institutions' activities and seeks every opportunity to reach an amicable settlement of disputes by launching new investigations to identify problems and promote good practice. the presence of a mediator, ready and willing to resolve disputes and differences between citizens, facilitates the processes of communication and coexistence between people with different ideas, experiences and projects. this is the starting point for strengthening and promoting this figure in europe so that there is good promotion and fair administration of the service.
in writing. - i think that, in the interest of fairness, parliament should have listened to commissioner verheugen's arguments on the merits of the case. i do not think i can therefore express any criticism of him. however, i support the ombudsman's position, as i believe that cooperation between the institutions is and should continue to be one of the strengths of the ombudsman's own work. in this respect, the late replies and the evasion of obligations which are not legislative but moral, indicate a reprehensible attitude. the construction of social capital, in putnam's view, goes beyond the lawfulness of behaviour, to look at the good faith, consistency and morality of the same. therefore, whatever the commissioner's motives, my solidarity goes without doubt to the ombudsman.
in writing. − the special report of the european ombudsman following the draft recommendation to the european commission concerning complaint 676/2008/rt was voted on in plenary today. in march 2007, a non-governmental organisation active in the field of environmental protection requested access to certain documents under regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 regarding public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. the european parliament, on behalf of the committee on petitions, supports the criticisms of the european ombudsman and his recommendation to the commission on complaint 676/2008/rt and recognises that the excessive delays in responding to the ombudsman on this issue constitute a breach by the commission of its duty of sincere cooperation under the tfeu. furthermore, the committee on petitions is of the opinion that the commission's lack of cooperation on this and other issues concerning access to documents risks undermining citizens' trust in the commission and undermining the ability of the ombudsman and the european parliament to supervise the commission adequately and effectively.
in writing. - for reasons of demographics, i have no memory of the days of the state monopoly on radio and television services and, in all honesty, i do not miss it. although the enormous barriers to entry eventually restrict the entry of new players into the market and therefore competition in this sector is in any case restricted for structural reasons, i have personally witnessed a considerable evolution in competitiveness in the television publishing sector. that being so, i do not think that an exclusively public system is even conceivable, since this would only further reduce the efficiency gains that competitors can make, to the detriment of consumers. on the other hand, a purely commercial television channel may not be interested in pursuing general interest objectives, such as the broadcasting of educational content, which is not always rewarding in terms of audience but is necessary by its very nature. the dual system must therefore be maintained, provided that there are rules to allow free and healthy competition and that there is no collusion between public and private companies, while respecting editorial choices but being aware of the social role that the broadcasting service must play.
in writing. - i have spoken in favour of mr belet's report on public service broadcasting. europe has now entered the digital age and the institutions must ensure a balance in the dual system established between private and public commercial broadcasters. the system of television and radio stations' ratings, which are able to influence public opinion as a whole, is worth all that. the adaptation of eu funding for the public broadcasting system of the member states is crucial because it is directly linked to the democratic, social and cultural needs of each society, as well as to the need to preserve media pluralism and to ensure diverse information and freedom of expression. as this is a matter for national authorities, the eu wants to see more incentives for public service broadcasting in order to revive a service that in many countries suffers from the burden of information policy and control and to avoid imbalances with sometimes unfair private competition.

in writing. the multiplier effect of the pollination phenomenon, i.e. the ratio between the economic value of the pollination itself and the honey produced by it, leads to exceptional results from an economic point of view. it is therefore counter-intuitive, in an age of efficiency in all its forms, to abandon an activity in which the cost-benefit ratio shows the folly of such a choice. as the reasons are not to be found in economic parameters but rather in external conditions, i think the committee's report is a good one in that it seeks to tackle all the factors which currently hamper beekeeping. i also believe that it is worthwhile to encourage this activity by means of accompanying measures, and i think it is necessary to welcome any scientific contribution to this end.
in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, beekeeping is one of the agricultural exploitation models with the least environmental impact and is therefore an activity particularly suited to protected areas. in my region, the widespread use of beekeeping is not only a good example of land management but also a testimony to the history, tradition and identity of the area. for many years, beekeeping in veneto has produced high-quality products and has contributed to the livelihood of the most disadvantaged areas. however, the sector cannot continue to deliver these results without the european union's contribution to its financing, in cooperation with the national, regional and local levels of government. as the motion for a resolution states, it is important to encourage research into bee diseases and to support european producers in the competition they face with third countries after the eu market is opened to honey imports. i shall therefore vote in favour of this proposal.
in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on beekeeping because it is important to ensure that attention is paid to a sector which protects biodiversity and produces a complete foodstuff such as honey. this role has led to an increase in the annual contribution to the sector in europe from eur 26 million for the period 2008-2010 to eur 32 million for the period 2011-2013. this funding will be used to support beekeeping, including through national research projects on new methods of combating the high mortality of bees, which has recently reached alarming levels. on the other hand, however, it is important to ensure fair transparency in the distribution of aid and to guarantee more resources to the states which actually need them. i voted in favour of implementing the data census system by 2012. a move towards transparency, so that aid is distributed on the basis of the census data of the hernias in the various member states and not on the basis of estimated data. i thought this was extremely important in order to ensure fairness for public spending and protection for those who actually practice the fishing business.
in writing. - the worryingly increasing bee mortality and the declining number of beekeepers could have very negative consequences on european food production, since, as we all know, the majority of crops and plants depend on pollination. it is therefore appropriate that this parliament should ask the european union to increase its support for the beekeeping sector in view of the renewal of the common agricultural policy. we need to take strong and concrete action to combat this phenomenon and to prevent its negative effects on our economy, both in the agricultural and commercial sectors. the action plan called for in the resolution to combat bee mortality is only the first of a series of measures that must be taken. my vote is in favour.

in writing. - after the climate, energy and food crises, the international financial crisis, which has led to a social crisis everywhere, only increases the need for strong rules to ensure that the world economy is better regulated and does not develop to the detriment of societies. international trade, which is at the heart of globalisation, is not exempt from this requirement. for citizens everywhere, the development of international trade is justified only if it contributes to economic development, employment and an improvement in living standards. it is only on this condition that the opening up of trade is experienced as positive and accepted. on the other hand, it provokes very strong opposition when it destroys jobs or calls into question living conditions, social rights and the environment. trade policy cannot therefore be reduced to the immediate interests of a few economic operators. for europe, trade policy must be consistent with all the union's objectives, in particular those of its foreign policy, of which it is one of the levers to promote the concept of a regulation of globalisation.
in writing. − a healthy market economy cannot do without continuous and constant monitoring of the state of competition within itself. however, such control cannot take the ideological form of a set of parameters which apply to everyone. the situation in each market niche must be examined on a case-by-case basis in order to make a fair assessment of compliance with those principles which, applied mechanically, would end up in paradoxical and uneconomic situations. the commission's attempt to control horizontal cooperation in specialization agreements and in research and development agreements, two rather sensitive areas whose peculiarities justify the confidential treatment to which they are subject, should therefore be appreciated.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on 18 december 1990 the un adopted the international convention on the protection of the rights of all migrant workers and members of their families. the convention is one of the nine principal human rights instruments of the united nations. unfortunately, after 20 years, none of the member states of the european union has signed or ratified the convention. i believe that the recognition of the rights of third-country nationals who live and work regularly in the european union must be a priority for a europe facing the new challenges of integration, non-discrimination and the protection of human rights. i therefore ask all members to support amendment no 16 and to sign the written declaration 96 which i have signed with cornelia ernst, sylvie guillaume and franziska keller to call for the member states to ratify the un convention on migrant workers.

in writing. i share much of mr juvin's views on the impact of advertising on consumer behaviour. however, i believe that the prevention of the dissemination of comments on social networks, forums/blogs - which by their very nature risk becoming a modern type of 'hidden advertising' - can be implemented by identifying the new forms of illegality favoured by the internet and by extending the regulation of the 'archiving of data to online content providers', rather than invoking forms of censorship, as i consider it a priority to respect the right of every citizen to be able to express his opinion also on the internet, when it is not proven that it violates the law. i am surprised that anyone would think of censoring a comment on a forum that is believed to be able to influence consumer purchasing choices, and instead consider the proposal to extend the current directive 2006/24 on data retention to allow the detection of paedophiles who harass children through social forums to be a violation of citizens' privacy. two weights and two measures? consumers, especially younger consumers, must be protected from hidden advertising. nevertheless, freedom of expression, which is one of the pillars of our democracies, must be proportionately protected. i therefore hope that the competent authorities can be provided with the necessary tools to identify the perpetrators of internet crimes by extending directive 2006/24 to content providers, as already requested in parliament's statement p7_dcl(2010) 0029 of 23 june 2010.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank, together with the rapporteur, all the members of the committee who have worked on these matters and all the members who have the future. i think that the commission's annual report on the application of the charter, which will take up a little bit of all the remarks that have been made by both sides on specific called it, this system of prevention whereby action in a member state would be intervened in until the action was launched. i have had my experts analyse this and the institutional issues raised by such a mechanism are very complex. for the time being, but we will have to continue the analysis and see what is really going on, it seems to me that there is no legal basis for this and that a change in the treaty would be necessary to enable such a preventive mechanism to be activated. the idea is attractive. we will continue to look for what mechanism could be used without changing treatment to address the most pressing. i would like to draw your attention to the fact that the charter is not applicable in the absolute sense, because this is a mistake that is often made. it is only applicable when member states put european rules into practice, for example when a european directive, which was agreed between the council and parliament, is subsequently incorporated into european law. at that point, the charter applies, but it does not apply in the absolute sense. in the absolute sense, that is to say, in all other cases, the national courts have the responsibility to intervene. when the european union becomes a member of the council of europe convention, there will be an additional dimension that we will then have to put into practice in the way we manage rights policy. this seems to me to be of paramount importance, beyond all the specific questions that have been asked - and i will answer them individually to the members who have asked them - i think the big question is the fundamental question. the charter is not yet fully understood by the outside world, in our member states and by governments. we must therefore inform the public so that there is a culture of rights and a policy of values throughout europe, so that everywhere, when laws are made and when they are applied, people ask themselves whether they are in accordance with the values we have subscribed to, that is, we as politicians must ask ourselves almost systematically, when we act, whether what we are doing is compatible with the fundamental rights we have subscribed to. this seems to me to be the most important element. i can tell you that today the commission is going to take a decision on the abolition of the exequatur, that is to say, a proposal will be put forward so that judicial decisions can circulate freely throughout europe. this is a decision of major importance. and for the first time, when proposing this new regulation, we examined the respect of fundamental rights, not just in terms of economic analysis, in terms of the impact on the market, but also in terms of the impact on values. as you can see, we are gradually moving towards this new policy and i think that we should, between the commission, the council and this house, make sure that this annual report on the application of the charter, which i will be presenting on behalf of the commission and which parliament will criticise or approve, becomes a great moment of truth and offers an opportunity to put everything to rest. it is also a matter of really showing the outside world, our voters, that, yes, the charter is alive. the charter is not just a text, it is a practice. and if it is not put into practice, the elected representatives of the people will say so loud and clear. that is what we must try to achieve in the two or three years before the next elections. i think we can achieve this gradually with the first exercise of this kind in the spring and then the establishment of a tradition in this house so that no one can ever again say when on wednesday or thursday you will be dealing with human rights outside the union. "you haven't put your own house in order". let's do it together!

the agenda includes the report by teresa jiménez-becerril barrio and carmen romero lópez, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and gender equality, on the draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on the european protection order (00002/2010 - c7-0006/2010 - 2010/0802 (cod)) (a7-0354/2010).
the s&d group has been represented. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with this proposal for a directive for which i am very grateful to the rapporteurs with whom i worked as a shadow rapporteur parliament shares and extends the council's proposal to protect in all 27 member states persons who are subject to forms of persecution or to serious and repeated threats by known and identified persons, often former fiancés or former spouses or partners, who endanger their physical integrity, dignity, personal freedom or sexual integrity. the violence and killings are increasing, especially of women whose threats and complaints have often been underestimated by the police and the judiciary itself, but at present protection orders and measures against the aggressor are only valid in the issuing state. commissioner reding, this measure which is being approved may not be perfect, but it fills a legislative gap! the construction of the european area of freedom, security and justice has always been carried out empirically, sometimes with the necessary coercion. we consider this initiative to be important because it will enable citizens of the union, men and women, and all those living in europe to move freely across borders, bringing with them their rights as persons and their rights to protection and security, as stated in article 3 of the treaty of lisbon, which we in the s&d group would have liked to have as a legal basis to give a more coherent meaning to the implementation of the proposal. the establishment of the ope guarantees that the protected person is also protected in the other member states, through a rapid and free procedure. each member state shall identify a competent authority responsible for informing victims of their rights, promoting campaigns, collecting analytical statistics and informing the person when the national protection order is issued. it also gives a strong impetus to the creation of the european legal area and the implementation of freedom of movement, but also applies for the first time the legislative initiative procedure in co-decision between the council and parliament. i hope that the council will confirm this commitment and i hope that the commission, while showing particular attention to the next package on safety for victims, will not miss this specific opportunity to respond today to the very serious situation also demonstrated by european and national statistics. this could lead, among other things, to important legislative convergence between member states. i therefore suggest that we avoid delays and make a specific commitment to this particular type of victim protection.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, there is no doubt that this directive on the european protection order for victims also marks an epochal step towards providing concrete guarantees for women in particular, but - as has already been said - not only for them. the guidelines for this measure had already been drawn up, first by the treaty of lisbon and then by the stockholm programme. i would like to applaud the two rapporteurs, mrs teresa jiménez and mr romero lópez, for their diligent work and the many difficulties they encountered in the council to give a meaningful impetus to this particularly important proposal for an area of freedom, justice and security that is really serving the citizen. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem, and i am sure that the council will take them into account. the fact that the measures are ready, timely and effective suggests that they can also be used to protect the victim's family. we look forward to the commissioner's more detailed package on the protection of victims of violence, which will arrive in the coming weeks. i would like to conclude, madam president, by saying how important it is for the practical implementation of this measure that close cooperation between the member states be combined with a high degree of sensitivity, and how important it is not to forget the importance of psychological support for the victims. i am sure that the commission will take this into account in the final stage of this legislative process.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i very much appreciate the work done by the two rapporteurs, but the problem with this draft directive is that it is based on the most typical model of stalking, where one person has been the victim of violence by another person and therefore we must take steps to protect him from the repetition of any form of physical or moral violence. it is obviously a matter of fundamental importance to hundreds of thousands of women in the eu and that is why i fully support its content. unfortunately, these provisions do not take into account the victims of organised crime, who in most cases are not to be defended by an identified or identifiable person, but by organisations which certainly cannot be notified of a restrictive measure. i therefore think that the european parliament should regard this directive as a first step in the implementation of the stockholm programme. i think that the rapporteur herself, mrs jiménez, and the commissioner herself are guided by this principle, in that they expressly refer to measures to protect victims of crime. i appeal to the european commission because in the package of measures on the protection of victims, planned for 2011, we also want to protect victims of organised crime and victims of crime at european level.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, i did not intend to speak again, but what has been said needs to be corrected. the measures which will be part of the victims package include an overarching communication, the lisbonisation of the 2001 framework decision on the standing of victims in criminal proceedings, a proposal on civil protection measures and, if necessary, a proposal on criminal protection measures. this will be put on the table of this house in may next year. we cannot just go ahead and put our ideas on paper. all our proposals must be accompanied by a thorough impact assessment. we need to take this very seriously, aiming for sound studies with real added value. that is what we are doing at the moment. we are finalising the impact assessment in order to determine the details of any actions on legislative and practical measures, with the aim of legal certainty and rapid and efficient protection measures. having said that, i would also like to inform this parliament that, to date, four opinions have been sent by national parliaments on the protection order: positive ones from the italian, greek and portuguese parliaments and a negative opinion from the german bundesrat arguing that the directive goes beyond the scope of article 82, as it covers non-criminal measures and the prevention of crime. it has been rejected on the basis of subsidiarity. we are in the middle of a very complicated issue. by carrying out a serious analysis before putting the legal and non-legal proposals on the table, i will try to propose measures which are sound enough not to victimise victims a second time when it comes to protection measures.

the agenda includes the report by mrs edit bauer and mrs anna hedh, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the prevention and repression of trafficking in human beings and the protection of victims of trafficking, repealing framework decision 2002/629/jha (com (2010) 0095 - c7-0087/2010 - 2010/0065 (cod)) (a7-0348/2010).
on behalf of the efd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, human trafficking is now, according to estimates by international organizations and police authorities, the second largest source of profit for organized crime worldwide, after drug trafficking. it is estimated that some 30 million people are victims of organ trafficking, prostitution, and forced labor. this means that the fight against this crime of vast proportions is first and foremost a battle for the safety of our citizens against the underground and against the crime that breeds crime. in the face of a phenomenon of this magnitude, europe rightly needs to take drastic measures against those who exploit human beings in various ways. in order to combat this phenomenon, cooperation between the member states and between the police authorities is necessary, but above all the certainty of penalties for traffickers; however, it must be remembered that many people are exploited because they cannot find decent living conditions in their home countries, they live in poverty and despair and are ready to do anything to leave their land for the promise of a better life, which - alas - will not come true. so, in addition to preventing crime and protecting the victims of trafficking, europe must do more and more diligently to ensure that these people can find acceptable living conditions in their own countries. the principle of 'help them at home' must be the guiding principle of european political action, so that our efforts are directed not only towards repression but also towards prevention!
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the gender dimension introduced in this proposal for a directive strengthens its instrument for the protection of the most vulnerable individuals. the fact that the lisbon treaty contains numerous references to trafficking in human beings confirms the timeliness and seriousness of the problem. article 5 (3) of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union prohibits the practice of slavery, equating it with a form of slavery and forced labour. the rapporteur has extended the protection with a particular focus on children and women and the conditions of vulnerability which facilitate this form of slavery. it is also right to point out that human trafficking is concealing forms of illegal adoption, forced marriage. i cannot help mentioning the difficulties faced by the border member states in combating illegal immigration. my country, italy first, is confronted daily with the repression of the cases of trafficking that invade our streets, our spaces. communication and therefore awareness raising, involving civil society, is needed; the text, as it stands, provides for the careful protection of victims and aims to eradicate the phenomenon. i therefore express my support for this proposal as it has been put forward and i congratulate the two rapporteurs once again.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as a shadow rapporteur i thank the rapporteurs and i consider this directive to be of extraordinary importance, because it is the first binding action of the union in the fight against trafficking in human beings. fifty years after the un convention, in our civilized europe, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly women and children, are enslaved. for the first time, the eu has a single instrument to tackle trafficking in human beings for both sexual and labour exploitation, including forced begging. three were the priorities of our group: target traffickers with uniform and higher sanctions, including confiscation of assets and their use in support of trafficked persons; ensure a high level of protection and social reintegration of victims with free legal assistance and non-prosecution for trafficking-related offences; enhance the crucial role of ngos, both secular and religious, engaged in supporting victims. i would, however, like to see a revision of the 2004 directive on residence permits for victims, and i would stress that we are proposing to safeguard the best interests of the child by means of enhanced safeguards, and i share commissioner malmström's wish for further measures against sex tourism and child pornography.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased that in the final version participation in criminal organizations for crimes relating to trafficking in human beings represents an aggravating factor which doubles the minimum sentences from five to ten years of imprisonment. article 6a is added, which explicitly refers to the seizure and confiscation of the instruments and proceeds of such crimes. this approach, which i believe is correct and which i hope will be translated into other legislative measures, faces reality and recognises that trafficking in human beings for various forms of exploitation, such as prostitution, criminal activity and organ trafficking, is carried out by international criminal organisations. i am also satisfied with the provision in article 7 which directs member states not to prosecute persons involved in criminal activities which they were forced to commit precisely because they were victims of trafficking. in fact, often the victims of trafficking violence, in addition to the damage, suffer the mockery of being incriminated for what they were forced to do, typical is the case of prostitution. that is why i support the report and thank the two rapporteurs.
madam president, the scourge of human trafficking is a phenomenon which has reached particularly worrying proportions. if originally it concerned mainly women and children recruited for prostitution, today the victims are subjects of all ages and both sexes, inserted in a cycle of exploitation not necessarily sexual but also economic. organized crime networks exploit social vulnerability, family hardship, domestic violence and disability to facilitate immigration by exploiting those involved through the use of force, abuse and threats. we are in favour of the proposed directive. the sanctions against human traffickers must be increased by confiscating their property. in addition, there should be joint action by all member states to strengthen policies to prevent trafficking in human beings by promoting the training of personnel capable of identifying victims or potential victims.
member of the commission. − madam president, thank you for this important debate. i would like to inform you that today the commission will appoint an anti-trafficking coordinator, who will take office in the next month. that person will improve coordination and coherence between the eu institutions and agencies and the member states, will help ensure that best practices are shared in the different member states, develop existing and forthcoming policies and be a contact for third countries. this is very important. by bringing together prevention, law enforcement and victim prevention, this person can ensure that appropriate methods to combat trafficking are used and mobilised appropriately. i will ask the anti-trafficking coordinator to liaise closely with the european parliament and to keep you informed on these developments. the criminalisation issue merits a debate in itself, but it is stated in article 19 of the directive that the commission will in some years submit a report to the european parliament and the council ‘assessing the impact of existing national law criminalising the users of services which are the objects of exploitation of trafficking in human beings on the prevention of trafficking in human beings, accompanied, if necessary, by adequate proposals’. we will surely come back to this issue and i do not rule out our having further proposals on this. having said all this, i think we can be proud of this directive today. it is a very important tool for fighting trafficking and protecting the victims. it has given us an important tool, it has shown the world our commitment to fighting modern slavery and it will strengthen our efforts. i would like to pass on my sincere thanks to the two co-rapporteurs, ms bauer and ms hedh. today’s debate has shown how important your work has been, because you have the support of all the groups. i would like to congratulate you on that.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place in a few minutes today. the commission shall be assisted by the committee of the regions.
in writing. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, human trafficking, in its various forms such as sexual exploitation, illegal trade in human organs, forced labour and illegal adoption, is a serious violation of human rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the scale of this phenomenon is significant and experience has shown that the current union legal framework in this area is not sufficiently effective; the cooperation between the european parliament, the commission and the council is therefore of strategic importance in promoting a european policy to combat this phenomenon effectively. the lisbon treaty has strengthened the european union's powers in the area of judicial and police cooperation between member states in criminal matters, but i still believe that it is necessary to increase sanctions for human traffickers and to further develop assistance to victims of violence. i agree that, in order to discourage demand, the union and the member states should make a greater effort, including through the organisation of awareness campaigns in the countries of origin, transit and destination of trafficking. finally, i encourage the establishment of a european anti-trafficking coordinator to manage the european union's action and policies in this specific area.
in writing. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union's action against trafficking in human beings is not limited to denouncing it, but recognizes the need for precise ex-post action to ensure that those responsible for such a barbaric practice do not go unpunished. these include the harmonisation of penalties and the coordination of the measures envisaged by the union with those already taken by other international organisations such as the united nations. ex-post action must be accompanied by equally important preventive action. firstly, close cooperation between the judicial and financial police authorities to ensure that the economic systems which revolve around these criminal activities are blocked at the outset and all their ramifications are cut off. it is also increasingly important to have accurate and reliable databases that distinguish the various specificities and become the starting point for diversified interventions that will affect each individual case in depth. with this proposal for a directive, the european union wants to strike at the whole chain of inhumane trade which tramples on its founding principles and values.
in writing. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, every year in europe hundreds of thousands of people are sold as objects and fortunately today the need to protect victims of human trafficking from the use of false documents, prostitution or immigration is growing more and more. when we talk about human trafficking, we must not only think about sexual exploitation, forced labour, illegal adoption but also about the problem of organ trafficking which is becoming an increasingly widespread crime. the european legal framework is not effective enough and the european union and the member states need to do more: a consolidated coordination structure is needed between the union institutions and agencies as well as between member states and international partners.

in writing. - my decision to vote in favour of report a7-0326/2010 goes hand in hand with the current situation of european capitals, which are going through a period of innovation, unprecedented thanks to technological progress. the implementation of mifid, which promotes competition between trading venues for execution services, has increased the efficiency of the price formation process, thus broadening the choice of investors. however, fragmentation of markets has clouded the post-trade transparency of otc transactions and this situation requires a more effective regulatory framework to achieve consolidated post-trade information. i believe that regulators should be able to reconstruct every moment of trading in order to understand the market dynamics and the way in which participants intervene. the impact of new technologies and the emergence of new market participants has led to faster trading and to the opening of direct market access to clients of trading platform members. although the implementation of mifid has brought innovation, it also appears to have contributed to market fragmentation. i voted in favour of the report because i believe that these technological advances must be properly regulated to avoid creating systemic risks for the whole market.
in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i fully support the rapporteur, mr kay swinburne, and his idea of promoting competition between trading platforms for execution services has widened investor choice, reduced transaction costs and helped to increase the efficiency of the price formation process. there are currently 136 alternative trading systems (mtfs) which, together with the main exchanges, constitute the organised trading venue system. this system accounts for 60% of the trading volume, while the remaining share is covered by independent intermediaries (broker-dealers) collectively referred to as otc. bilateral trading - where the client transmits an order to the broker and the broker matches the order - which used to be mainly verbal, is now mainly carried out electronically. the commission considers that the mfi's reporting requirements are not sufficient to ensure that the mfi's reporting requirements are met.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the vote in the ep on the proposal for a directive establishing a european protection order for victims is an important signal for the defence of persons who are victims of violence. unfortunately, even if the council lacked a qualified majority after the netherlands sided with the countries blocking the initiative, this will not affect the importance of today's vote. the legislative vacuum at european level in the protection of victims of violence requires a concrete response, not confined to the territory of the state in which the victim is present, but extending beyond its borders. the aim of the collaboration of 12 member states, including italy, is to activate a mechanism for alerting and protecting victims within the european territory. i am convinced that it is important, even politically, to reach agreement on this instrument, because it will guarantee protection for victims of all types of crime and provide for removal and interdiction measures against persons who pose a danger. equally important is the possibility for the victim to move to another member state, receiving the information and assistance he needs to start a new life, while continuing to benefit from protection measures.

in writing. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a directive on the european protection order, thanks to the contribution of the council, but above all to the two rapporteurs and to the amendments we have proposed in the commission, represents an excellent instrument for the protection of victims without any limitation on national legislation, and this must be noted as a symbol of regulatory progress in a europe which is trying to standardize rights and protections in each of its member states "step by step". the european protection order instrument as presented makes the protection of the victim who wishes to move freely within the european union more precise and timely. the limit of the diversity, even operational, of our legislative systems is clear, but the scope as defined allows our countries to adapt quickly to the new instrument, thus making our union stronger and protecting the citizens of europe better, especially the most vulnerable. that is why i strongly support this proposal, which would give hope to the many people who see their freedom and dignity violated every day without having all the means to react and who may even be able to start their lives again in another country in the future.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on the draft european parliament and council directive on the european protection order because the eu needs a system that strengthens the protection of the life, safety and physical, mental and sexual integrity of citizens who are the victims of attacks. the proposal for a directive aims to strengthen the protection of victims of such crimes within the eu, as protection measures are limited to the domestic legislation of the member states. the resolution seeks to fill a legislative gap in which the victim of aggression is protected outside his own country, thus ensuring that each member state offers the victim adequate protection. the member states will have no obligation to harmonize their internal legislation but may adapt it in order to ensure mutual recognition.
in writing. - i congratulate mr jiménez-becerril and mr romero lópez on the excellent work they have done. victims of crime who are entitled to protection in one member state will be guaranteed the same level of protection across the union, thanks to the new european protection order (epo), approved today, which extends the scope of the rules to include all victims of crime, not just victims of gender-based violence as originally proposed. protection measures exist in all eu member states, but they lose their effectiveness as soon as you cross a border. the european protection order should ensure that any protection granted to a person in one member state also applies in all other member states to which he or she moves or has moved. the european protection order may be issued at the request of the person to be protected if he or she decides to reside in another member state, or if he or she simply decides to stay there. it will be for the state which issued the protection measure to issue an ope and to forward it to the state where the person intends to go. the text still needs to be confirmed by a qualified majority of the member states in the council, which will have three years to transpose it into national law.
in writing. - there is nothing more inhuman than to exploit the lives of other living beings for personal gain, trampling on the respect of every fundamental right. human trafficking is one of the lowest forms of human trafficking in history, a widespread and multifaceted phenomenon. i am glad that parliament has approved the proposal for a directive on trafficking in human beings at first reading. this is a major step forward in the fight against this phenomenon, which is the main activity of many international criminal organizations. the most important point is the recognition of organized crime as the main subject to be combated. finally, the eu proposes effective and concrete distinctions between crime and organised crime, taking account of the specificities of the latter. there are many other positive aspects, such as a much broader definition of exploitation, greater protection for victims and the rule that avoids victims of trafficking being prosecuted for crimes they were forced to commit because of the violence they have suffered or the threat of violence. as amnesty international reports, 'it is often the case that trafficked women are arrested on the charge of prostitution or that they are not guaranteed full access to justice'.
